17948021463300196.caption:
How my schedule changed as my agency grew:

0-20 clients:

I was doing everything. Fulfillment, strategy, sales calls, content, audits for every brand in the pipeline. All of it ran through me.

This is the phase where you learn the business inside and out because you literally have no choice. You are the business.

20-50 clients:

This is where everything almost broke.

I was still doing fulfillment and managing all the client strategy myself and it wasn't sustainable. So I made the hardest shift: I gave up fulfillment.

Brought on a Director of Ops to take the lead on client work execution.

A big shift was starting hiring people who actually had experience instead of just whoever I could afford. 

Then you get people to oversee them. You build a layer between you and the day-to-day work.

I was able to double down on content, marketing, and sales. Still had my hands in fulfillment a little bit. But the shift was happening.

50-100 clients:

Now I was still working 12-14 hours a day still.

I had to ask myself a real question: what do I keep doing myself?

The answer was marketing. That was the thing that I’m best at and viewed as highest leverage.

My hardest decision was dropping sales… but it was necessary as I was spending 4-5 hours a day on it.

I brought on a closer and spent a stupid amount of time training him up and managing him. Over time though, this become a huge time unlock.

And still, a ton of my time went into hiring and escalations, all while keeping up with all the marketing I was doing. 

100+ clients:

Now it's about building the machine that runs without me in it.

Training up senior team members on email strategy so the quality stays high without me reviewing every account. 

My time goes into content, overall company development, and building new things. 

My next phase is getting sales management off my plate, sales audits off my plate, service development off my plate, and working closely on developing AI systems.

The work never gets less… (I’ve worked 10-12 hours a day every day since I started)…

It just changes.

At every stage you have to be willing to let go of the thing you were good at so you can focus on what you need to grow.

17978876262141245.caption:
Comment “SUBSCRIPTION” for the full 30+ page subscription document! 

1. Get first orders on subscription. First order subscribers are worth 2-3x more than one-time buyers at the 12 month mark. 

2. Front load your subscription offer. Instead of 20% every order, do 30% off first order and 10% recurring. We incentivize first order subscription and save margin on back end. 

3. Auto select subscription on your PDP page. This automatically increases your subscription take rate. Very little effort with high impact. 

4. Align pop-up offer with subscription offer. No need to give an extra discount. Just have your pop-up offer be your best subscription offer. Save margin. 

5. Have a strong email onboarding. Have multiple emails educating on long term usage of product. Get them to use the product every day. And get them to buy in to 6 month+ of usage. 

6. Customize billing reminders emails. Change the framing from “you’re about to be charged” to “get excited, here’s what’s coming”.

7. Customize order confirmation emails. Instead of framing being “you were just charged” make it “congrats, here are the benefits you have” 

Comment “SUBSCRIPTION” for the full 30+ page subscription document!

18113358068324038.caption:
The thing holding your business back is probably you thinking nobody is as good as you.

There was a time I was managing like 20 accounts at one point…

And I kept telling myself that if I handed anything off it would be worse, the client would get a worse experience, and the work would suffer.

So I just held onto everything.

Then one day I literally did not have the time to do it anymore. So I told my account manager to just present their strategy and emails to the client.

I was bracing for the client to be disappointed…

Turns out they loved it. They even told my AM they liked it better than what I had been doing.

That messed with me for a while because in my head their work was WORSE than mine.

But the client didn’t see it that way at all.

It was different for sure.

But different doesn’t always mean worse.

”80% done by someone else is 100% awesome” - Dan Martell

If someone can get something to 80% of how you would do it that’s 100% awesome. Because the time it takes to go from 80 to 100 is not worth it. And most of the time nobody notices the difference except you.

The moment I actually bought into this was when the business started growing.

Because I stopped holding onto everything and started letting people own their work while I could focus on getting clients.

You can’t scale if every piece of output has to go through your brain first.

Agency owners will try to add a new service every 6 months and wonder why nothing scales lol

I’ve been doing email marketing for years now… Just email.

Every year there’s been a reason to expand into something else.

Ads, web design, SEO, start a SaaS, whatever.

And every year I have just said no and went deeper on email.

We’d rather be the best at one thing than average at five.

And because of that we now manage 100+ brands, have 100+ employees, and have generated over $250M in email revenue for our clients.

I get why people do it… It feels like you’re leaving money on the table.

But the ability to say NO and stay focused on improving what you already have is a skill.

Why try to learn and start something new from ground 0… when you could just add fuel to what’s ALREADY WORKING… ?

The ones doing whatever they can get their hands on end up doing 6 things at a 5/10 instead of one thing at a 10/10.

I’m sure we’ll be doing more here pretty soon… but it will be as a result of extreme patience and timing the market right.

18039986558839048.caption:
A one-star review feels personal, so the first reply most owners write is a defense. Three paragraphs on why the customer is wrong.

The person who left it is already gone. The people reading your reply are deciding whether to buy from you next week, and they’re reading it to find out what kind of company they’d be dealing with. A long argument tells them more about you than the review did.

So I’d fix the thing first, if it’s real, then write two lines:

You were right. It’s been fixed.

If it isn’t real, the reply is still two lines: stay polite and say what you’d do for them next time.

A quick check: read the last three replies you wrote and ask whether you’d buy from the place that wrote them.

18078891650559655.caption:
Every founder I know can tell a friend what their business does in one sentence. Then they sit down to write the website or a post, and it comes out as “bespoke lifestyle solutions.”

People give you about two seconds. If they can’t tell what you do in that time, they’re gone, and more words only bury the one thing that would have told them.

So I’d write the plain version first:

What you do and who it’s for, in the words a customer would use. You can dress it up later, as long as a stranger can still tell it’s a bike shop.

Quick test: read your headline to someone who doesn’t know what you do and ask them to say it back. If they can’t, it isn’t done.

I’d rather have customers who buy because they want what I sell than customers who only show up for the discount.

A discount works the first time. Run one every week, and people learn that the sale price is the real price, so they stop buying until the next one.

Look at the last ten messages you sent your customers. If most of them were about a discount, that’s what they’re waiting for now.

A welcome offer for new customers is fine. But for the people who already buy from you, the reason to come back shouldn’t always be a lower price.

Give them a new product, a limited run, something that’s only around for a few days. Put that in most of the next ten messages instead.

Plus a few extra tips:

• Opens are inflated by privacy features, so judge subject line tests by clicks.

• Put one useful product tip in the order confirmation. People open it to check their order, so make it count.

• Send the founder note from a real inbox and read the replies. “Why’d you pick us?” answers are some of the best ad copy you’ll find.

• If shipping is slow, say so early. A heads up cuts down on “where’s my order?” emails.

• Hold the cross-sell until after it arrives. Let them love the first thing before you pitch the second.

• Split out repeat buyers. Skip the founder note for them and send a short thank-you for coming back instead.

18098943149428056.caption:
hills i’ll die on after generating over 8+ figures for brands

after building email for brands across every niche, these are the principles i keep coming back to every single month:

→ attributed revenue is a skewed metric: your email platform can take credit for sales it didn’t actually drive.

→ plain text beats designed emails: designed emails look beautiful, but plain text cuts through the noise because it reads like a real person wrote it.

→ spend 80% of your time on the hero section: most people never scroll past the first screen, so the top of your email decides whether the rest even gets seen.

→ send more emails: good content doesn’t annoy people, and just like on social media, nobody unfollows a creator for posting great stuff every day.

→ unsubscribes are a good thing: the people leaving were never going to buy, and every unsubscribe helps you land in the inbox for the ones who will.

→ copy paste your winning angles every month: most of your list never saw your best email the first time, so if it worked once it will work again.

→ good popups never hurt conversion rates: bad popups do, but a good one captures visitors who were going to leave anyway.

→ you own your list, not your followers: algorithms change overnight, but your list lets you reach every customer whenever you want.

the point isn’t to follow every email “best practice” you see online, it’s to understand what actually moves revenue and ignore what only looks good in a report.

because great email marketing isn’t about sending prettier emails, it’s about understanding how people actually buy.

Sometimes it’s the smallest details that make an email feel more personal.

One thing I like adding to welcome flows is a short note from the founder.

Literally only a few sentences that introduce the person behind the brand and give subscribers a reason to connect with them.

Here’s a quick framework you can steal:

1. Introduce yourself
“Hey, I’m [Name], the founder of [Brand].”

2. Share why you started
“I started [Brand] because [the problem you wanted to solve].”

3. Make it about the customer
“Our goal is to help you [specific benefit your brand provides].”

4. Give a personal thank you
“Thanks for being here. It seriously means a lot.”

5. Remind them about their welcome offer (if you have one)
“In case you missed it, your [OFFER] is still available.”

6. End with a CTA
“Shop with your [OFFER] here>>”

Throw in a photo of the founder and their signature, and you’re good to go.

You don’t need to write an entire essay. 4–6 sentences that actually sound like you is enough.

Save this for the next time you’re updating your welcome flow.

Steal this $6,000,000 Email Strategy 👀

1. Pop-Up Form 📋

-Show it after 6–8 seconds and keep every step stupid simple
-Use a micro-commitment before asking for their email
-Make the offer impossible to miss
-Cut fluff like “exclusive news & updates”
-Keep A/B testing the offer until you’re around 10%+ opt-in

2. Campaigns 📤

-Send 3–4x per week at minimum
-Build every email around ONE small topic
-Mix education, product, social proof, brand, and sales
-Lean into seasonality instead of constantly discounting
-Mix in plain-text and visual/infographic-style emails

3. Flows 📥

-Welcome: 5–6 emails
-Site Abandon: 1–2 emails
-Browse / Cart / Checkout: 3–5 emails
-Build Post-Purchase + Winback too
-Keep pre-purchase emails about 1 day apart
-Put abandoned products near the top and test different offers

Getting more traffic is obviously great.

This system is what helps you actually make more money from them.

It’s the same framework we’ve used to generate over $6M through email for our clients.

18131594531496507.caption:
Retention is what builds a brand… If your customers only buy once, you’re not building a brand. You’re renting them.

Most e-commerce brands are obsessed with acquisition.

But what happens after someone makes their first purchase?

If they never come back, you’re stuck paying to acquire another customer just to replace them.

And that can create a dangerous cycle where your growth becomes entirely dependent on how much money you can keep pumping into advertising - not necessarily a bad thing & you can still be profitable (but it’s not building a brand if they buy once & never again)

Because when you increase customer retention:

→ You can afford to spend more acquiring customers.

→ Your profitability improves

→ You build a loyal customer base

→ You become less dependent on paid advertising to survive.

The brands that win long term aren’t necessarily the ones acquiring the most customers.

That’s how you build a brand, not just a store.

18074379611412521.caption:
👉 Lessons after generating over $100m+ in email revenue

Lesson 1 — The offer beats the email

You can write the best email in the world, but it won’t work if the deal isn’t exciting.

Example:

A skincare brand sends a beautifully designed email offering 10% off one product. It barely makes any sales.

They change the offer to:

“Buy the full routine and get the cleanser free.”

The copy and design stay almost the same but sales jump because the offer is stronger.

Takeaway: Before rewriting the email, improve what you’re asking people to buy or how you position it.

Lesson 2 — Timing beats frequency

Sending more emails to everyone isn’t as powerful as sending the right email at the right moment.

Example:

A customer views the same protein powder three times but doesn’t buy.

Instead of waiting for the next general campaign, the brand automatically sends:

“Still deciding? Here’s what makes this formula different.”

It answers their questions while the product is still on their mind.

Takeaway: Customer behaviour tells you when and what to send.

Lesson 3 — Your best customers shouldn’t receive the same emails as everyone else

Different customers need different reasons to buy.

Example:

A first-time visitor might need:

“Get 15% off your first order.”

But a loyal customer who has purchased six times doesn’t need another discount. They might respond better to:

“You’ve got early access to our new product.”

One customer needs a reason to try the brand. The other wants recognition and exclusivity.

Takeaway: Change the message based on the customer’s relationship with the brand.

Lesson 4 — Attributed revenue isn’t the same as generated revenue

Email platforms can take credit for orders that the email didn’t actually cause.

Example:

An abandoned-cart flow says it generated $100,000.

The brand excludes a small test group from receiving those emails. That group still spends $70,000 because many customers return and buy anyway.

The email’s true extra impact was closer to $30,000, not the full $100,000 shown in the dashboard.

Takeaway: Measure the extra sales caused by email—not just the sales it received credit for.

18120817759892721.caption:
Follow these tips to become an email marketing powerhouse 👇

1) Define the customer pain point
If you don’t know what your customer is struggling with, your email is guessing.

2) Make emails that are aesthetic
Good design signals a serious brand. Bad design gets deleted.

3) CTA above the fold
If they have to scroll to find the button, most of them won’t.

4) Create segments for every customer
Talking to everyone means connecting with no one.

5) Send at least 12 emails per month
The brands doing real numbers are sending way more than you think.

6) Check flow performance every week
Your flows print money in the background. Ignoring them is leaving cash on the floor.

7) Turn off smart sending
Klaviyo’s default settings are throttling your reach. Take back control.

8) Implement pattern interrupts
The email that looks different in the inbox is the one that gets opened.

9) Use infographics
Your customers scan. They don’t read. Design accordingly.

10) Reuse your winners
If an email worked once, it’ll work again. Stop reinventing every send.

Your discount popup might be costing you sales.

When someone signs up for a discount, they’re ready to buy. But if your welcome email takes an hour to arrive, they might be gone before the code does.

Test it yourself: Open your store in a private browser, sign up through your popup, and time how long the email takes to arrive. Aim for 1–2 minutes.

Even if the popup displays the code, send it by email too. Customers need an easy way to find it when they’re ready to check out.

18111250766265169.caption:
“I refuse to pay $6 for shipping,” she says, and adds a $12 pair of socks to her cart.

Most of us have done some version of this.

Before she added the socks, her cart was $44. Free shipping started at $50, and the store had $12 socks hanging right next to checkout. All of that was planned.

She walks away feeling like she beat the system, and the store just added $12 to her order.

If you’re setting this up, start with how much a typical customer spends per order. Use the median, since a few big orders can inflate the average. Set your free shipping minimum a little above that. Then, in the cart, show how far people are from free shipping and suggest a few small, useful items that get them there.

After that, check two things: that the extra profit from bigger orders covers the shipping you’re now paying for, and that the free shipping minimum isn’t so high that people give up and leave.

In a Bizrate Insights survey earlier this year, 56% of US shoppers said they expect free shipping once they spend $25 to $49, so most people already have a number in mind.

18125514212516601.caption:
Spend five minutes scrolling Instagram, and it's easy to feel behind.

Someone just hit a milestone.
Someone just announced a big launch.
Someone seems to be growing twice as fast.

I came across an idea called "The Turtle Theory" that I really like.

Its message is simple:

Slow progress is still progress.

A few reminders that stuck with me:

1. Small steps add up.

Especially when you take them consistently.

2. Someone else's timeline isn't your deadline.

You get to move at your own pace.

3. Taking a break doesn't erase your progress.

Sometimes you need to rest, reset, and come back with a clearer head.

4. Progress isn't always visible.

Better habits, clearer thinking, and more patience are wins, too.

5. Your confidence should come from within.

You shouldn't need constant praise or approval to feel good about where you're headed.

6. Moving slowly doesn't mean you're stuck.

A thoughtful step forward still moves you closer to your goal.

This applies to building a business, getting healthier, raising a family, or working through a tough season.

Some days you'll sprint.

Other days you'll take one small step.

Both count.

Keep going.

18149807236565181.caption:
A lot of brands spend October rebuilding their welcome flow for Black Friday.

It won’t make you a single dollar of extra revenue in November.

If anything it costs you money, because the signup discount stacks on top of your Black Friday offer.

Here’s the flows that actually matter during BFCM, in the order I’d work on them:

Post purchase
Most important flow in any Klaviyo account, any time of year. For Black Friday, the main job is setting the expectation that delivery might take longer than usual but will still arrive before Christmas. This saves you hundreds of “”where’s my order”” emails.

Browse abandonment
Highest volume flow during Black Friday, and a lot of the time it generates most of the flow revenue. Everyone is shopping multiple brands at once so the follow up matters.

Abandoned cart

Active on site

Heaps of people are browsing in November without clicking a product. This catches them. #klaviyo

18106110557628265.caption:
The first thing in your Black Friday email should be the offer.

Not a brand photo. Not a lifestyle shot. The offer and the deadline.

That’s all people care about this time of year. We’ve had emails that are literally a black background with “”40% off, ends Monday”” and a button, and they do really well.

A few other things to get right:

? Link to a collection, not one hero product. We want people to click through and browse for what they want, not have us tell them what they want.

? Show buy now pay later options. People lean on Afterpay a lot in Q4. It can get expensive, so keep an eye on it.

? If you have a big catalogue, add a live bestsellers section that updates as things sell out.

? Redesign your flow emails so they look like Black Friday too. Just remember the message matters more than how it looks.

If a customer has to scroll to find the deal, you’ve lost them. #klaviyo

18120133457073433.caption:
The Christmas shipping cut-off and Boxing Day were the original Black Friday before Black Friday was a thing.

So the worst thing you can do after Cyber Monday is relax.

Here’s what I’d be doing in December and January:

Get your Black Friday buyers to a second order

This is the big one. You just picked up a wave of new customers at a discount. If you don’t get them back in the first 60 days, you won’t hear from them until next Black Friday. If at all.

You have to be very intentional about this. Post purchase content, a clear next product, and a reason to come back that isn’t another 30% off.

Run a December gifting angle

Works every year. People are still spending, they’re just buying for someone else now.

Refresh your flows in January

Probably the only time of year you’ll actually have time to do it.

What I wouldn’t do is extend your sale into January.

Discounts only work when they’re rare. Extending just pushes the fatigue later and trains your customers to wait for the next one. #klaviyo

18126363905299189.caption:
Most of the churn tactics I see subscription brands using are about catching people on the way out.

Pause, skip, a 30% off win back...

They all have a place. But by the time someone’s clicked cancel, you’ve already lost most of the battle.

The thing that actually moves lifetime value is what happens in the first 90 days.

If a new subscriber gets a proper onboarding sequence that tells them how to use the product, what to expect and when, they don’t get to the cancel button in the first place.

So if I was ranking where to spend your time:

Fix your 90 day onboarding sequence. Biggest impact on LTV by a mile.
Add a delay option to your billing reminder. The reminder lands on the day people are most likely to cancel, so give them “”push my order back”” instead of “”cancel””.
Build a failed payment recovery flow. Quick to set up and catches a lot of people who never meant to leave.
Pause and skip at the cancel step.
Win back discounts. Gets some people back but doesn’t fix why they left.
Most brands do this in reverse order. #klaviyo

17953056282308031.caption:
Flat 20% off sitewide was the worst performing Black Friday offer across all our brands last year.

The problem is that people can do the math in the subject line. They already know what they’re saving, so there’s no reason to click through and browse.

Here’s what actually worked, best to worst:

Up to 30% off

Best performer across the board. You put the biggest discount on slow moving stock and the smallest discount on products people were going to buy anyway. So you clear stock without giving away margin on your best sellers.

Spend more, save more

Pushes up basket size, and customers who spend more on their first order are much more likely to come back. The only downside is the customer has to do a bit of math.

Chance to win a refund / free gift with purchase

I wouldn’t run either as the main sale offer. But they’re good cards to have on hand when daily revenue starts to slow down mid sale and you need to reignite it.

Flat 20% off sitewide

See above.

No sale at all

You don’t have to discount on Black Friday. But you do need to run some kind of promotion, otherwise you’re just donating customers to your competitors for the biggest shopping week of the year. #klaviyo

18035737298891616.caption:
When a subscriber cancels, Klaviyo and Recharge will tell you that they cancelled.

They won’t tell you how fixable it was.

Here’s the 5 reasons we see most often, ranked from easiest to hardest to fix:

1 / Card declined

These people didn’t even decide to leave. You just need to follow up and remind them to update their card. Easiest money you’ll make all month.

2 / Too much product

They like the product, it’s just arriving faster than they can use it. Let them change the frequency and most of them stay.

3 / They felt it didn’t work

This is an expectations problem. If someone signs up for a supplement or skincare, they need to be told what results look like at week 2, week 4 and week 8. Otherwise they cancel in month 1 thinking nothing happened.

4 / It worked

You can’t stop someone leaving because their problem is solved. What you can do is cross-sell them onto your other products while they’re still a subscriber, so when they cancel one they stay on for the rest.

5 / They came for the discount

There will always be a few. But if it’s a big chunk of your cancellations, your front-end offer is bringing in the wrong people and you need to change it.

If you’re trying to reduce churn, start at the top of this list, not the bottom. #klaviyo

If you run a subscription brand, Klaviyo attributed revenue is the worst number you can look at.

It counts revenue that was going to happen anyway.

Here’s the metrics I’d look at instead:

→ First order subscription take rate

What % of first time customers choose subscription instead of one-time. This is one of the most important numbers in the whole business, and most brands don’t track it.

→ Order 3 retention

Most brands track order 2. But you can hack order 2 with a discount and it doesn’t actually increase LTV. You can’t hack the third order. That’s why order 3 is much more correlated with lifetime value.

→ Cancel reasons

Not really a metric, but it tells you exactly what’s broken in your onboarding sequence.

Total subscriber count is the number everyone wants to grow, but it’s a lagging indicator. It tells you how last quarter went, not what to do next. #klaviyo

18126543509309116.caption:
Flat 20% off sitewide was the worst performing Black Friday offer across all our brands last year.

The problem is that people can do the math in the subject line. They already know what they’re saving, so there’s no reason to click through and browse.

Here’s what actually worked, best to worst:

Up to 30% off

Best performer across the board. You put the biggest discount on slow moving stock and the smallest discount on products people were going to buy anyway. So you clear stock without giving away margin on your best sellers.

Spend more, save more

Pushes up basket size, and customers who spend more on their first order are much more likely to come back. The only downside is the customer has to do a bit of math.

Chance to win a refund / free gift with purchase

I wouldn’t run either as the main sale offer. But they’re good cards to have on hand when daily revenue starts to slow down mid sale and you need to reignite it.

Flat 20% off sitewide

See above.

No sale at all

You don’t have to discount on Black Friday. But you do need to run some kind of promotion, otherwise you’re just donating customers to your competitors for the biggest shopping week of the year.

18116261069588558.caption:
Most of the churn tactics I see subscription brands using are about catching people on the way out.

Pause, skip, a 30% off win back...

They all have a place. But by the time someone’s clicked cancel, you’ve already lost most of the battle.

The thing that actually moves lifetime value is what happens in the first 90 days.

If a new subscriber gets a proper onboarding sequence that tells them how to use the product, what to expect and when, they don’t get to the cancel button in the first place.

So if I was ranking where to spend your time:

Fix your 90 day onboarding sequence. Biggest impact on LTV by a mile.
Add a delay option to your billing reminder. The reminder lands on the day people are most likely to cancel, so give them “”push my order back”” instead of “”cancel””.
Build a failed payment recovery flow. Quick to set up and catches a lot of people who never meant to leave.
Pause and skip at the cancel step.
Win back discounts. Gets some people back but doesn’t fix why they left.
Most brands do this in reverse order. #klaviyo

18637590859025569.caption:
When a subscriber cancels, Klaviyo and Recharge will tell you that they cancelled.

They won’t tell you how fixable it was.

Here’s the 5 reasons we see most often, ranked from easiest to hardest to fix:

1 / Card declined

These people didn’t even decide to leave. You just need to follow up and remind them to update their card. Easiest money you’ll make all month.

2 / Too much product

They like the product, it’s just arriving faster than they can use it. Let them change the frequency and most of them stay.

3 / They felt it didn’t work

This is an expectations problem. If someone signs up for a supplement or skincare, they need to be told what results look like at week 2, week 4 and week 8. Otherwise they cancel in month 1 thinking nothing happened.

4 / It worked

You can’t stop someone leaving because their problem is solved. What you can do is cross-sell them onto your other products while they’re still a subscriber, so when they cancel one they stay on for the rest.

5 / They came for the discount

There will always be a few. But if it’s a big chunk of your cancellations, your front-end offer is bringing in the wrong people and you need to change it.

If you’re trying to reduce churn, start at the top of this list, not the bottom. #klaviyo

18113173073155846.caption:
6-figure and 8-figure founders use the same tools.

Same flows. Same pop-up. Same Klaviyo.

The difference is the thinking behind every decision.

→ 6-figure: “”I have an abandoned cart flow.””
→ 8-figure: Cart, checkout and browse flows, split by new, returning and VIP customers.

→ 6-figure: Pop-up asks for email, name, phone number and the dog’s name.
→ 8-figure: Asks for everything, but only the email is required.

→ 6-figure: Emails the whole list.
→ 8-figure: Aggressive to people who want more emails. Backs off everyone else.

→ 6-figure: “”We’re at a 10 ROAS.””
→ 8-figure: Breaks even on the first order on purpose, because they know exactly what a customer is worth over their lifetime.

→ 6-figure: Sends a discount to bring people back.
→ 8-figure: Sends value when customers are due to reorder. Only discounts once they’ve churned.

→ 6-figure: “”Klaviyo says it made $80k last month.””
→ 8-figure: Ignores that number and tracks returning customer revenue.

Retention is what lets the 8-figure brand outbid everyone on acquisition.

Breaking even on the first order only works if you’ve nailed the second.  #klaviyo

18212558587363375.caption:
Pop-up offers, ranked 1 to 5.

10% off → 3

The default. It works, everyone uses it, nobody gets excited about it.

Free gift with purchase → 4

When you crack it, it’s brilliant — the cost price is usually cheaper than the discount you’d otherwise give.

But you rarely crack it. Most brands don’t have the right gift sitting there.

Mystery discount → 2

Still works surprisingly well. People will click a mystery box.

Free shipping → 5

Customers expect free shipping now. You can’t trade someone their email address for a thing they already assume they’re getting.

Chance of a refund on your first order → 1

Best pop-up offer running right now.

Everyone who signs up and buys goes into a draw. Every month or quarter, you refund one of them.

To them: a shot at a completely free order.
To you: a net discount under 1%.

Converts as well as 10% off, sometimes better, at a fraction of the cost. #klaviyo

18122793460903445.caption:
Let’s compare the three pop up offers we see brands run.

Offer 1: 10% off

$100 AOV. You give 10% off.

You keep $90. Customer gets $10 of value.

Offer 2: Gift with purchase

Same $100 AOV. Instead of a discount, they get a free tie with their first order.

Costs you $5. Retails at $50.

You keep $95. Customer gets $50 of value.

On paper it’s a win win. More money for you, more value for them.

But in practice this used to smash it in 2022 and 2023 and it just doesn’t work like it used to. For us it generally performs worse than a straight 10% off now.

Offer 3: A chance at a full refund

This is the best performing pop up offer I’ve seen.

Customer still spends their $100. The pop up says sign up for a chance to have your entire order refunded.

At the end of the month you pick one order, refund it, and make an event out of it.

One refund across a thousand orders costs you about 10 cents an order.

You keep basically your full $100. The customer gets to punt. People love to punt.

Obviously don’t run this if gambling doesn’t sit right with your brand.

But if it does, nothing else comes close. #klaviyo

18633373012016146.caption:
4 things brands get wrong in their welcome flow.

Don’t make people go to their inbox to claim the discount code.
Show the discount on the popup itself so they can check out on site. You already got the email. Don’t trade a guaranteed sale for it.

Don’t send one welcome email.
Minimum 4. Add SMS on top.

Don’t leave smart sending on.
Turn it off in your core flows. These people are at their most likely to convert, so the last thing you want is a setting quietly skipping them.

Don’t send the same templated email four times.
Vary the message and the format so it stays fresh for the reader.

Someone joining your list is the most interested in your brand they will ever be.

Build the flow like you know that. #klaviyo

18100255520072689.caption:
4 things brands get wrong with offers and discounts.

Don’t give $5 off a $400 item.
It’s not enough to move anyone. Offer a gift with purchase instead.

Don’t make your welcome discount bigger than your subscription discount.
Keep the offer consistent. If the popup beats subscribing, nobody is ever going to subscribe.

Don’t let discounts stack by accident.
Set exclusion rules and make them clear, so customers aren’t confused at checkout.

Don’t start Black Friday earlier every year.
Hold the window. Every early launch teaches your audience that the urgency is fake.

Your offer isn’t just a number on a popup.

It’s a promise about what your product is worth. #klaviyo

18034337921899843.caption:
Never, ever test your pop-up button colour.

I’ve seen brands burn weeks on it. It does nothing.

Here’s what actually moves your pop-up conversion rate:

→ Headline copy — you can make real swings just by rewriting this
→ Fields on slide one — too many and people get overwhelmed and bounce
→ Mobile optimisation — your pop-up is the same as everything else, it’s getting seen on a phone
→ The offer — the single biggest lever you’ve got

And the one almost everyone gets wrong:

Put the discount code in the pop-up itself.

If you force people to go check their inbox for the code, your website conversion rate drops and your email conversion looks amazing. That’s not a win. That’s just moving revenue from one report to another.

Never sacrifice website conversion in the exact moment your customer is on your site, just to get someone to click an email.

Button colour is not your problem. The offer is. #klaviyo

18117291374051940.caption:
The founder of True Classic said it straight on LinkedIn:

“”We acquire customers at break-even and rely on our product to bring them back.””

They’ve scaled ad spend at break-even and let repeat customers bring in the profit.

Here’s why that works 👇

First order → maybe 10-15% margin.

Second order →
→ Bigger carts
→ No ad spend to get them back
→ Margin closer to 40-50%

Stack a few repeat purchases and the profit adds up fast.

The first order buys you the customer.

Retention is where the profit comes from. #klaviyo

18136532434648022.caption:
Most good brands have all the flows they need.

Where they go wrong is not personalising them.

Take an abandoned cart:

→ First-time visitor? A few emails, then maybe a discount to get them over the line. Klaviyo will say it worked great.

→ Customer who’s bought from you 10 times? Do they need a discount?

Probably not.

They know you. They love your products. They use them religiously.

You don’t need to give away margin to get them back.

Use urgency instead.

Or remind them about all the loyalty points they’ve built up.

Same flow, different customer, different message. #klaviyo

18105012026249344.caption:
Go to the websites for Huel or AG1 a few times.

The pop-up is constantly changing.

Same offer. Different format.

They’re always testing to find the highest converting version.

And once the top brands have your email?

They get very aggressive.

Grüns sent 6 emails in a 24 hour period.

I’m not saying you need to do that.

But it’s more proof of something we see in every account:

People are the most interested they’ll ever be when they’re in your welcome series.

Don’t waste that window being polite. #klaviyo

17990976837024701.caption:
The active on site flow is your safety net.

It triggers when someone is on your website but doesn’t click a single product.

Lower intent than browse abandonment, sure.

But the moment someone visits your site, your competitors start retargeting them.

So you need to follow up too.

Position it like a helpful shop assistant:

Email 1 → “”Need a hand?”” Show your most popular categories, or the main pains you solve.

Email 2 → Recommend specific products your customers usually love.

It catches people who slip through all your other flows. #klaviyo

18116152580072594.caption:
If I could only have one flow, it’d be the post-purchase flow.

Right after someone buys online, there’s a little voice in their head:

“”Did I just make a bad decision?””
“”When’s it going to arrive?””
“”Can I trust this company?””

Leave that voice unchecked and you get chargebacks and bad reviews.

Here’s how we shut it down:

1. Immediately → “”We’re packing your order now.”” Not just the default Shopify receipt.

2. A few hours later → Invite them to your Instagram / Facebook so they can see the brand is real.

3. Next → Something educational. Styling tips for clothing, recipes for food, where to spray for fragrance. Help them get more out of it when it arrives.

4 & 5. 10-14 days after the order (when it’s actually arrived) → Ask for a review or push an upsell.

Give value first.

That’s what earns you the right to ask for more. #klaviyo

Browse abandonment will be one of your highest volume flows.

It triggers when someone views a product but doesn’t add to cart or checkout.

Lots of people do that, but they haven’t shown much buying intent yet.

So the strategy is a soft nudge, not a hard sell.

Email 1 → “”We saw you looking at this. We’ve set it aside for you.”” Add a bit of urgency so it doesn’t get snapped up.

Email 2 → Show your main collections and categories. If that product didn’t grab them, something else might.

Emails 3-4 → You can offer a discount here.

But I generally don’t.

Save your margin for people who actually show buying intent. #klaviyo

18141662545719944.caption:
Open rates don’t matter.

There’s no correlation between open rate and revenue.

Here’s the proof:

Send an email only to people who opened in the last 2 days.

You’ll get an 80-90% open rate.

But you’ve only sent to 100 people, so it makes no money.

You can push your open rate up or down just by changing who you send to.

So why track it at all?

Deliverability.

If revenue was all we cared about, we’d send to the full list every day. That would wreck our inbox placement.

So we want open rates:

→ High enough that Gmail, Yahoo and Hotmail see us as a quality sender
→ Low enough that we’re sending to as many people as possible

The safe zone is roughly 35-50%.

Above that? Send to more people.
Below that? Tighten your segments. #klaviyo

17989195731047674.caption:
From auditing hundreds of Klaviyo accounts:

80% of brands don’t have their abandoned cart flow set up properly.

They think they have one.

It’s actually a checkout started flow.

Here’s how to check in 30 seconds:

→ Open your abandoned cart flow in Klaviyo
→ Look at the trigger metric
→ If it says “”Checkout Started””, you don’t have an abandoned cart flow

A real abandoned cart flow triggers on “”Added to Cart””.

That’s one step before checkout, and it catches people who never even made it there.

Go check yours. #klaviyo

18382975708226061.caption:
List fatigue isn’t really a thing.

The idea is that if you email too much, people get bored, stop opening and unsubscribe.

What we actually see is closer to the opposite.

Sending too little, or sending inconsistently, does far more damage.

The worst pattern?

→ Send a bunch of emails one week
→ Go quiet for a couple of weeks
→ Come back hard for a sale

That hurts list health, engagement and unsubs more than sending 5-6 emails every week.

I’m not saying send 5-6 a week.

3-4 is usually the sweet spot.

But whatever you pick, stay consistent. #klaviyo

18198908500348623.caption:
Most people think subject lines drive open rates.

They don’t.

Run a subject line A/B test, get a “”winner””, then run the exact same test a few months later.

It’s a coin flip whether the result holds.

That basically makes it meaningless.

Our only rules for subject lines:

✅ Sound like a human, not a corporation
✅ If you do A/B test them, pick the winner on sales, not opens

Stop overthinking your subject lines.  #klaviyo

18115489913519766.caption:
Your welcome flow is the most important flow in your Klaviyo.

When someone signs up is the most interested they’ll ever be in your brand.

The longer they sit on your list, the less likely they are to buy.

Most brands only send 1-2 welcome emails. That’s not enough.

Here’s the minimum we build:

1. Immediately → Re-send the discount code. Nothing else. Make it easy to go back and buy.
(Not opened? Resend after 3-4 hours with a new subject line.)

2. Day 1 → Plain text email from the founder. Who you are and why you started.

3. Day 2 → Social proof. Reviews, testimonials, customers loving the product.

4. Day 3 → Us vs them. Why you’re better than competitors.

5. Day 4 → Handle the common objections people have before buying.

If the last email still makes money, add another one.

Seems aggressive?

This is the most interested they’ll ever be. Use it. #klaviyo

18105979475255497.caption:
We’ve worked with 150 clients.

Across every one of them, the best performing campaigns are always one of three things:

→ A sale
→ A product launch
→ A back in stock email

Every single business.

What do they have in common?

They’re all news.

Something is actually happening, and the brand is just telling customers about it.

Nothing converts better than news.

So if your calendar is all “”5 reasons to love our product”” emails, find more real news to send. #klaviyo

18076048808564485.caption:
The number one reason people cancel a subscription is they have too much product.

Yet the most common save offer I see is a discount on the next order.

Which just means more product turning up that they don’t need yet.

Here’s what works much better:

Let them delay the next order by 2, 4 or 6 weeks.

It solves the actual problem, and they stay on subscription instead of starting from zero.

A few other things brands try:

Pause instead of cancel - a pause is a cancel unless you force them to pick a restart date.

A handwritten card from the founder after they cancel - leaves a great impression, but hard to say if it actually brings anyone back.

Hiding the cancel button or making people email you to cancel - borderline illegal, and you’ll never win that customer back.

Fix the reason they’re leaving. Don’t just make it cheaper to stay. #klaviyo

18027617054866609.caption:
The Christmas shipping cut-off and Boxing Day were the original Black Friday before Black Friday was a thing.

So the worst thing you can do after Cyber Monday is relax.

Here’s what I’d be doing in December and January:

Get your Black Friday buyers to a second order

This is the big one. You just picked up a wave of new customers at a discount. If you don’t get them back in the first 60 days, you won’t hear from them until next Black Friday. If at all.

You have to be very intentional about this. Post purchase content, a clear next product, and a reason to come back that isn’t another 30% off.

Run a December gifting angle

Works every year. People are still spending, they’re just buying for someone else now.

Refresh your flows in January

Probably the only time of year you’ll actually have time to do it.

What I wouldn’t do is extend your sale into January.

Discounts only work when they’re rare. Extending just pushes the fatigue later and trains your customers to wait for the next one. #klaviyo

18132737881773690.caption:
Flat 20% off sitewide was the worst performing Black Friday offer across all our brands last year.

The problem is that people can do the math in the subject line. They already know what they’re saving, so there’s no reason to click through and browse.

Here’s what actually worked, best to worst:

Up to 30% off

Best performer across the board. You put the biggest discount on slow moving stock and the smallest discount on products people were going to buy anyway. So you clear stock without giving away margin on your best sellers.

Spend more, save more

Pushes up basket size, and customers who spend more on their first order are much more likely to come back. The only downside is the customer has to do a bit of math.

Chance to win a refund / free gift with purchase

I wouldn’t run either as the main sale offer. But they’re good cards to have on hand when daily revenue starts to slow down mid sale and you need to reignite it.

Flat 20% off sitewide

See above.

No sale at all

You don’t have to discount on Black Friday. But you do need to run some kind of promotion, otherwise you’re just donating customers to your competitors for the biggest shopping week of the year. #klaviyo

17989483272119657.caption:
Most of the A/B tests brands run in Klaviyo are a waste of time.

Button colour. Preview text. Sender name. How many buttons are in the email.

Whatever result you get probably won’t hold the next time you run it.

Same with subject line tests judged on open rate. Open rate doesn’t tell you which email made more money.

Here’s the tests that are actually worth running:

Send time

This has a measurable impact. Tradies check their phone at smoko, mums check before school pick up. Find when your customers actually open.

Send day

Also matters quite a bit.

Spend threshold vs flat % off

Eg. “”spend $100, get $20 off”” vs “”15% off sitewide””. This is one of the highest leverage tests you can run in email because it changes AOV and margin, not just clicks.

If a test can’t change how much money the email makes, don’t run it. #klaviyo

18115853798113463.caption:
Here’s what should be in the first email of your abandoned cart flow.

The only job of email 1 is reminding the customer why they were shopping in the first place.

So the most important thing in the email is their actual cart, with the checkout button right underneath it.

Then reviews. Star ratings, a verified badge, real customer names. One of the biggest reasons people don’t buy is they don’t trust you yet, and reviews solve that objection better than anything you can write yourself.

What I’d take out:

→ The lifestyle banner at the top. A picture of the product they abandoned will always beat a hero image.

→ Your brand story. That belongs in the welcome flow.

→ A discount code. Always try to get the sale without cutting into margin first. If you need an offer, bring it in at email 3 or 4.

Cart, reviews, button. Nothing else. #klaviyo

18100059026355745.caption:
The first thing in your Black Friday email should be the offer.

Not a brand photo. Not a lifestyle shot. The offer and the deadline.

That’s all people care about this time of year. We’ve had emails that are literally a black background with “”40% off, ends Monday”” and a button, and they do really well.

A few other things to get right:

? Link to a collection, not one hero product. We want people to click through and browse for what they want, not have us tell them what they want.

? Show buy now pay later options. People lean on Afterpay a lot in Q4. It can get expensive, so keep an eye on it.

? If you have a big catalogue, add a live bestsellers section that updates as things sell out.

? Redesign your flow emails so they look like Black Friday too. Just remember the message matters more than how it looks.

If a customer has to scroll to find the deal, you’ve lost them. #klaviyo

Spend more, save more

Pushes up basket size, and customers who spend more on their first order are much more likely to come back. The only downside is the customer has to do a bit of math.

Chance to win a refund / free gift with purchase

I wouldn’t run either as the main sale offer. But they’re good cards to have on hand when daily revenue starts to slow down mid sale and you need to reignite it.

Flat 20% off sitewide

See above.

No sale at all

You don’t have to discount on Black Friday. But you do need to run some kind of promotion, otherwise you’re just donating customers to your competitors for the biggest shopping week of the year.

18360837019220008.caption:
The first thing in your Black Friday email should be the offer.

Not a brand photo. Not a lifestyle shot. The offer and the deadline.

That’s all people care about this time of year. We’ve had emails that are literally a black background with “”40% off, ends Monday”” and a button, and they do really well.

A few other things to get right:

? Link to a collection, not one hero product. We want people to click through and browse for what they want, not have us tell them what they want.

? Show buy now pay later options. People lean on Afterpay a lot in Q4. It can get expensive, so keep an eye on it.

? If you have a big catalogue, add a live bestsellers section that updates as things sell out.

? Redesign your flow emails so they look like Black Friday too. Just remember the message matters more than how it looks.

If a customer has to scroll to find the deal, you’ve lost them.

18097059605400274.caption:
The Christmas shipping cut-off and Boxing Day were the original Black Friday before Black Friday was a thing.

So the worst thing you can do after Cyber Monday is relax.

Here’s what I’d be doing in December and January:

Get your Black Friday buyers to a second order

This is the big one. You just picked up a wave of new customers at a discount. If you don’t get them back in the first 60 days, you won’t hear from them until next Black Friday. If at all.

You have to be very intentional about this. Post purchase content, a clear next product, and a reason to come back that isn’t another 30% off.

Run a December gifting angle

Works every year. People are still spending, they’re just buying for someone else now.

Refresh your flows in January

Probably the only time of year you’ll actually have time to do it.

What I wouldn’t do is extend your sale into January.

Discounts only work when they’re rare. Extending just pushes the fatigue later and trains your customers to wait for the next one. #klaviyo

When starting out, I was copying everybody.

Copying their email strategies, outreach scripts, content strategies, etc.

A lot of subscription churn happens in the first few orders. Here’s 4 changes that help.

1. Don’t lead with a discount to get people onto the subscription
Announce a free gift the day box one lands, so they have a reason to stay for the next order.

2. Don’t wait for subscribers to pause or cancel
Offer them the chance to delay their next order so they can finish what they have before the next box arrives.

3. Don’t go quiet after the first order
Send a clear results timeline so they know what to expect after order one, two and three.

4. Don’t send the same “”update your card”” email every time a payment fails
Personalise it by how many times the card has declined. Once or twice could be an accident. Three or four times, treat them like a churned customer you’re trying to win back. #klaviyo

18189564250409093.caption:
If you want more first orders going onto subscription, a deeper discount is usually the wrong lever.

It just hurts your contribution margin. A 10% subscription discount on its own doesn’t do much either.

What actually moves take rate:

→ The subscription offer itself
→ Cadence options, so people can pick a delivery frequency that suits them. This one is very important
→ Saying “”cancel anytime”” loudly
→ Pushing the subscription offer in your pop-up, campaigns and flows, not just on the product page

One thing I’d avoid is stacking all the freebies on order one.

People subscribe, get everything on the first order, then cancel straight away. #klaviyo

18116059934328349.caption:
Before you film, think about the person you’re making it for. If you’re not sure they’d stop scrolling for this topic, pick one they’re already asking about.

The algorithm shows your video to more people when viewers keep watching. If they leave in the first few seconds, it stops pushing it.

A crowded niche just means people want that topic. What gets you noticed is a take, a story, or a style that’s clearly yours.

A good hook can’t save a topic that feels boring to your audience. Find the part of the subject that affects their life and lead with that.

People follow when they feel like they’ll miss something if they don’t. Give them a reason to want your next post.

Most people feel awkward on camera because they’re trying to sound like a creator. Talk like you would to one friend and it gets a lot easier.

When you expect views just for posting, every low number feels like failure. Posting gets easier when each video is a chance to learn something.

Ideas show up when you give yourself room to think. If most of your free time goes to scrolling other people’s content, there’s no space left for your own.

Posting a lot only helps if you look back at what worked and what didn’t. Pick one thing to change on your next video.

Each of these feels like the problem, but there’s a real cause underneath that you can fix. Start with the one that hit closest to home.

18114972926160182.caption:
The first thing in your Black Friday email should be the offer.

Not a brand photo. Not a lifestyle shot. The offer and the deadline.

That's all people care about this time of year. We've had emails that are literally a black background with ""40% off, ends Monday"" and a button, and they do really well.

A few other things to get right:

→ Link to a collection, not one hero product. We want people to click through and browse for what they want, not have us tell them what they want.

→ Show buy now pay later options. People lean on Afterpay a lot in Q4. It can get expensive, so keep an eye on it.

→ If you have a big catalogue, add a live bestsellers section that updates as things sell out.

→ Redesign your flow emails so they look like Black Friday too. Just remember the message matters more than how it looks.

If a customer has to scroll to find the deal, you've lost them. #klaviyo

18012563078770380.caption:
Billing reminders do increase churn. That’s just the reality of them.

The job is to test and reduce how much churn they cause.

What I’d put in a billing reminder:
- Clear information about the upcoming charge. This is legally required anyway
- A reminder of the benefits they’re getting
- Any free gifts coming up in their next order
- Personalisation by product

What I wouldn’t do:
- Leave the default reminder templates as they are
- Hide the cancel button. It’s bad practice and probably illegal

Then test how every change affects churn. #klaviyo

18640107616023318.caption:
The Christmas shipping cut-off and Boxing Day were the original Black Friday before Black Friday was a thing.

So the worst thing you can do after Cyber Monday is relax.

Here’s what I’d be doing in December and January:

Get your Black Friday buyers to a second order

This is the big one. You just picked up a wave of new customers at a discount. If you don’t get them back in the first 60 days, you won’t hear from them until next Black Friday. If at all.

You have to be very intentional about this. Post purchase content, a clear next product, and a reason to come back that isn’t another 30% off.

Run a December gifting angle

Works every year. People are still spending, they’re just buying for someone else now.

Refresh your flows in January

Probably the only time of year you’ll actually have time to do it.

What I wouldn’t do is extend your sale into January.

Discounts only work when they’re rare. Extending just pushes the fatigue later and trains your customers to wait for the next one. #klaviyo

18125689591908774.caption:
Getting a brand to $3M a year doesn’t need an advanced email setup.

Most of what people obsess over at this stage doesn’t matter yet.

What does matter:
- Welcome flow
- Abandoned cart
- Consistent campaigns
- Optimising the pop-up
- Send time optimisation
- Advanced segmentation

What doesn’t:
- Birthday flows
- Hyper personalisation
- A/B testing subject lines
- Building 15 flows
- A loyalty program
- A sunset flow. You don’t need to email unengaged people, you can just suppress them

Same with deliverability. You’re not sending enough volume at this stage for it to be a real worry.

Just don’t do anything stupid and you’ll be fine. #klaviyo

18106317215458246.caption:
10% off isn’t much of a reason to sign up to a recurring subscription.

But jumping straight to a bigger discount isn’t the answer either.

Here’s what I’d do:

1. Stack different offers, like a free gift, free shipping and a small discount
2. Before going deeper on the discount, compare the contribution margin of subscribers at 3 to 6 months with your one-time customers. That tells you what you can actually afford
3. Don’t put every freebie on order one. Space the gifts out over a few months so people have to stay subscribed to get them
4. Don’t offer a price guarantee. Guarantee stock instead, so subscribers get first allocation. It also gives a bit of FOMO that your product might sell out. #klaviyo

Some of your biggest Black Friday sales will come from the smallest list you email all November. That list is your early access waitlist.

How early access works
➡️ Spend 7 to 10 days hyping up your customers
➡️ Get them to join your early access waitlist
➡️ Announce the early access offer to them 1 day before your public sale launches

A waitlist like this converts anywhere between 20 and 60%. Where yours lands depends on how well you build the hype, with email and social working together so your customers see what's coming everywhere they look.

17995245857846924.caption:
Most brand owners think sending more emails means annoying their customers.

And if every email is another discount or “SHOP NOW” message, they’re probably right.

But the problem isn’t always how often you’re emailing. It’s WHAT you’re emailing.

Think about it.

If the only time your customers hear from you is when you want them to buy something, why would they want to keep opening your emails?

Instead, show them what makes your brand different.

Educate them on your products, share customer stories, answer common questions, or show them how to actually use what you’re selling.

When you have the right campaign strategy in place, sending 2–4 emails a week becomes a whole lot easier.

You’re giving them a reason to care about your brand

What I’d set up:

1. A cancellation splash page. It’s good at recovering people who were about to cancel
2. Pause or delay options
3. A cancellation reason survey. You learn why people leave, pre-solve those reasons in onboarding, and personalise how you follow up with each person
4. Personalised cancellation offers

What I wouldn’t do:

→ Offer everyone the same discount to stay. People cancel for different reasons
→ Run an email win back sequence straight after. These people have already checked out
→ Make cancelling harder. It’s borderline illegal, and it kills any chance of reactivating that customer later.#klaviyo

17916256113533963.caption:
Flat 20% off sitewide was the worst performing Black Friday offer across all our brands last year.

The problem is that people can do the math in the subject line. They already know what they’re saving, so there’s no reason to click through and browse.

Here’s what actually worked, best to worst:

Up to 30% off

Best performer across the board. You put the biggest discount on slow moving stock and the smallest discount on products people were going to buy anyway. So you clear stock without giving away margin on your best sellers.

Spend more, save more

Pushes up basket size, and customers who spend more on their first order are much more likely to come back. The only downside is the customer has to do a bit of math.

Chance to win a refund / free gift with purchase

I wouldn’t run either as the main sale offer. But they’re good cards to have on hand when daily revenue starts to slow down mid sale and you need to reignite it.

Flat 20% off sitewide

See above.

No sale at all

You don’t have to discount on Black Friday. But you do need to run some kind of promotion, otherwise you’re just donating customers to your competitors for the biggest shopping week of the year. #klaviyo

18120784882758244.caption:

→ Instead of bigger sitewide discounts to get people buying more, use hand-picked bundles that lift AOV and work for your margins
→ Don’t give VIPs discounts. They’d already buy from you at full price. Give them perks instead, like early access to new products and restocks, and exclusive events
→ Don’t upsell customers before their product arrives. Give value first, then upsell once it’s in their hands. #klaviyo

18637612228000398.caption:
Around day four of a Black Friday sale, revenue usually drops back to normal. A lot of brands react by raising the discount.

I wouldn’t.

Here’s how I’d plan it:

→ Don’t run 20% off sitewide. Use “”up to”” framing, with the biggest discount on slow-moving stock and the smallest on your hero products
→ When revenue drops, add a second offer on top of the first instead of raising the discount. For example, the next 100 orders go into a draw, or the next 100 orders get a gift
→ Plan two or three of those offers before the sale starts, so you can launch one as soon as sales dip, because they will dip. #klaviyo

18135038053674106.caption:
The quickest way to lift subscription take rate on a product page is to pre-select the subscription option.

That alone usually moves it straight away.

A few others that help:
- Show how much they save by subscribing
- Show the free gifts they get
- Match the delivery frequency to how fast people actually use the product

That last one matters most for churn.

If you deliver 60 days of product every 30 days, no email flow or strategy is going to fix your churn.

What doesn’t matter: button colours, fancy product descriptions, or making one-time purchase hard to find. #klaviyo

18231302665336476.caption:
The Christmas shipping cut-off and Boxing Day were the original Black Friday before Black Friday was a thing.

So the worst thing you can do after Cyber Monday is relax.

Here’s what I’d be doing in December and January:

Get your Black Friday buyers to a second order

This is the big one. You just picked up a wave of new customers at a discount. If you don’t get them back in the first 60 days, you won’t hear from them until next Black Friday. If at all.

You have to be very intentional about this. Post purchase content, a clear next product, and a reason to come back that isn’t another 30% off.

Run a December gifting angle

Works every year. People are still spending, they’re just buying for someone else now.

Refresh your flows in January

Probably the only time of year you’ll actually have time to do it.

What I wouldn’t do is extend your sale into January.

Discounts only work when they’re rare. Extending just pushes the fatigue later and trains your customers to wait for the next one. #klaviyo

18107204798573084.caption:
The job of your billing reminder email is to not cause a cancellation.

We’re happy if the customer takes no action from it at all.

Here’s how I’d set it up:

1. Don’t just put a cancel button in it. Give people the option to skip or delay their next order
2. Don’t make it all about the upcoming charge. Build excitement and remind them of the benefits they signed up for
3. Don’t add an SMS reminder on top. One email is enough
4. Don’t judge it on revenue. Track how many people cancel after receiving it and work to bring that number down. #klaviyo

18061255319635921.caption:
Most churn is decided in the first two weeks of a subscription.

That’s when people either build the habit of using the product properly, or they don’t.

If I’m working on churn for a subscription brand, here’s where I’d spend the time:

- An onboarding flow that helps people build that habit in the first two weeks
- A billing reminder flow. For a lot of brands this is the biggest cause of churn, so it has to be done well
- A splash page offer when someone goes to cancel. This recovers a lot of people
- Pamphlets in the packaging, so people have the information they need to use the product consistently
- Product quality

What I wouldn’t prioritise: win back flows, surprise and delight flows and payment failed flows.

Win back is you trying to get people back after you’ve already lost them. Most of the work should happen before that point. #klaviyo

18058859075571155.caption:
Comment “GREEN” to get 30% off omnisend for your first 3 months.

Your quietest subscribers are costing you inbox placement with everyone else. 

Email clients judge you on engagement, so every send to people who never open pulls you closer to the spam folder. 

The fix is sending most of your campaigns to a 30-day engaged segment.

Here’s what to include in your engaged segment:
✨ Subscribed to email as your first filter
✨ Opened or clicked an email in the last 30 days
✨ Started a checkout, added to cart or viewed a product in the last 30 days
✨ Every engagement filter joined with “or”, so 1 action is enough to get in
✨ Include as many website metrics as you have, so if cookies miss one, the next picks it up

#omnisend #emailmarketing

18237183616324025.caption:
This is how the Instagram algorithm works for non-followers.

When you post a video, Instagram will show it to 150 people who don't follow you... If people out of those 150 watch and engage with your video, Instagram will show it to other non-followers who have the same interests as the people who watched/engaged.

The next time one of these people opens their feed, they're going to see another one of your videos. If you have a lot of videos, it makes it easier for Instagram to show them a good video that matches their interests based on the first video of yours they saw.

At the end of the day, we can't expect people to follow us just from one viral video, but if they continue to see us every single day, eventually they will follow. I have people who have told me they have seen over 30 of my videos before they decided to follow. Think about that: someone saw me 30 times before they decided to hit the follow button.

Because I post 10 times per day, it makes it so much easier for Instagram to show my videos to more people who don't follow me but have engaged with one of my videos in the past. Not only am I making it easier for Instagram to show them more of my videos, but I'm also making it easy for Instagram to show them a similar video to the one they originally liked, increasing the chances that this person will eventually follow me.

Long story short, post more fucking videos.

You can sell the dream in your ads.

But once someone has bought, you need to be realistic about what they’ll get and when. Otherwise they cancel as soon as it doesn’t match what they were sold.

What I’d focus on in onboarding:

1. Setting realistic expectations
2. Teaching people how to use the product properly
3. Helping them build a daily habit with it
4. A welcome video from the founder. This one actually makes a difference

What I wouldn’t worry about: thank you emails, adding more emails after delivery, or fancy email designs. #klaviyo

18115223069137026.caption:
The first thing in your Black Friday email should be the offer.

Not a brand photo. Not a lifestyle shot. The offer and the deadline.

That’s all people care about this time of year. We’ve had emails that are literally a black background with “”40% off, ends Monday”” and a button, and they do really well.

A few other things to get right:

→ Link to a collection, not one hero product. We want people to click through and browse for what they want, not have us tell them what they want.

→ Show buy now pay later options. People lean on Afterpay a lot in Q4. It can get expensive, so keep an eye on it.

→ If you have a big catalogue, add a live bestsellers section that updates as things sell out.

→ Redesign your flow emails so they look like Black Friday too. Just remember the message matters more than how it looks.

If a customer has to scroll to find the deal, you’ve lost them. #klaviyo

18031076606864107.caption:
Most win back emails are a generic “”we miss you””. There’s no real reason in there to come back.

Here’s what I’d do instead:

1. Tell people what’s new, so there’s a genuine reason to be interested in your brand again
2. Don’t send every cancelled subscriber a discount. Ask why they cancelled and personalise your response to that reason
3. Skip the heavily designed email. Send a plain text note or a video from the founder

And don’t rely on a win back flow to increase lifetime value.

Pre-solve the reasons people churn, so fewer of them ever get to the point where you need to win them back. #klaviyo

17879288157567318.caption:
Average monthly churn is one of the most common subscription metrics. It’s also not specific enough to be useful.

Here’s what I’d track instead:

- First order subscription take rate. How many people you get onto the subscription in the first place
- Order 2 retention
- Order 3 retention. If someone makes it to 3 orders, there’s a good chance they’ll stay for 6
- Contribution margin per customer

I wouldn’t lean on revenue per subscriber or average subscription duration.

Duration gets messy because people renew at different frequencies, weekly, fortnightly and so on. #klaviyo

Flat 20% off sitewide was the worst performing Black Friday offer across all our brands last year.

The problem is that people can do the math in the subject line. They already know what they’re saving, so there’s no reason to click through and browse.

Here’s what actually worked, best to worst:

Up to 30% off

Best performer across the board. You put the biggest discount on slow moving stock and the smallest discount on products people were going to buy anyway. So you clear stock without giving away margin on your best sellers.

Spend more, save more

Pushes up basket size, and customers who spend more on their first order are much more likely to come back. The only downside is the customer has to do a bit of math.

Chance to win a refund / free gift with purchase

I wouldn’t run either as the main sale offer. But they’re good cards to have on hand when daily revenue starts to slow down mid sale and you need to reignite it.

Flat 20% off sitewide

See above.

No sale at all

You don’t have to discount on Black Friday. But you do need to run some kind of promotion, otherwise you’re just donating customers to your competitors for the biggest shopping week of the year. #klaviyo

Big brands start their Black Friday sales earlier every year. It moved to mid-November, then to the start of November, and now some brands start in October.

Small to medium brands don't need to follow them. We don't have the team to keep up that much hype, manage stock and produce promo material for weeks on end. Mid-November onwards is where you'll get your best results.

Never launch on Black Friday weekend. It's the busiest weekend of the year for emails and marketing, so your launch gets buried in the noise. Always launch before Black Friday day itself.

The 2 sale lengths I teach
➡️ The run-up strategy: 14 days
➡️ The weekend strategy: 6 days

How to choose yours
➡️ Look at what's happening in your lead-up. Product launches you can't move will push your sale start back
➡️ Look at your revenue goal. A big goal needs a longer sale to give you time to hit it
➡️ Be honest about your resources. If you can't support a long sale, keep it tight and adjust your goal to match

You don’t need to keep selling to them.

Things that hurt:

→ Sending them every sale

Things that help:
→ A subscriber-only newsletter

17906735037351123.caption:

- Don’t deepen the discount to get subscribers. Offer a stack of incentives that drips out over months, so people subscribe and have a reason to stay subscribed
- Don’t blast active subscribers with campaigns. Only send them information that helps them get better results from the product
- Don’t rely only on Meta and your product page. Build a dedicated post-purchase journey that turns one-time buyers into subscribers #klaviyo

17893904898617240.caption:
Black Friday works differently when a big part of your revenue is recurring subscriptions.

Give existing subscribers a sitewide discount and a lot of them will cancel their subscription and buy at the Black Friday price instead.

Here’s how I’d approach it:

→ Gifting offers. Buy more so you can give it to friends and family. This is the angle I’d take for most people on a subscription
→ Subscriber exclusive offers, with cross-sell items that actually add value
→ Add-on products in their next shipment

What I’d avoid:

→ Discounting their existing subscription orders
→ Excluding subscribers from every sale
→ Daily sale reminders to subscribers. This actively hurts you #klaviyo

18118218545033475.caption:
The first thing in your Black Friday email should be the offer.

Not a brand photo. Not a lifestyle shot. The offer and the deadline.

That’s all people care about this time of year. We’ve had emails that are literally a black background with “”40% off, ends Monday”” and a button, and they do really well.

A few other things to get right:

→ Link to a collection, not one hero product. We want people to click through and browse for what they want, not have us tell them what they want.

→ Show buy now pay later options. People lean on Afterpay a lot in Q4. It can get expensive, so keep an eye on it.

→ If you have a big catalogue, add a live bestsellers section that updates as things sell out.

→ Redesign your flow emails so they look like Black Friday too. Just remember the message matters more than how it looks.

If a customer has to scroll to find the deal, you’ve lost them. #klaviyo

17881851741545317.caption:
November is the month your email cadence naturally lifts. 

At the start of the month, the focus is engagement. Keep your list opening and clicking with no discounts until Black Friday.

At the end of the month, the focus is selling. From the moment you start building your early access waitlist to the moment your sale goes live, there will be a lot of emails going out. That's exactly what Black Friday needs.

Here's your November send overview:

1️⃣ Us vs them: put your product side by side with the alternative
2️⃣ Hero product: 1 product, the whole story, no discount code
3️⃣ Early access waitlist: give your best customers a reason to sign up early
4️⃣ Let them play: a quiz or guessing game to keep them engaged
5️⃣ Early access launch: your waitlist shops first, a day or 2 before everyone else
6️⃣ Black Friday live: lead with the offer and make it impossible to miss
7️⃣ Gift guide: turn your Black Friday offer into their Christmas list

The other things that matter at this stage:

→ First to second order conversion
→ VIP segment growth
→ Incrementality testing
