→ A proper segmentation strategy, which helps deliverability and returning customer revenue at the same time

Birthday flows still don’t matter here.#klaviyo

17908142061596670.caption:
Getting a brand to $3M a year doesn’t need an advanced email setup.

Most of what people obsess over at this stage doesn’t matter yet.

What does matter:
- Welcome flow
- Abandoned cart
- Consistent campaigns
- Optimising the pop-up
- Send time optimisation
- Advanced segmentation

What doesn’t:
- Birthday flows
- Hyper personalisation
- A/B testing subject lines
- Building 15 flows
- A loyalty program
- A sunset flow. You don’t need to email unengaged people, you can just suppress them

Same with deliverability. You’re not sending enough volume at this stage for it to be a real worry.

Just don’t do anything stupid and you’ll be fine. #klaviyo

17904904470603456.caption:
Around day four of a Black Friday sale, revenue usually drops back to normal. A lot of brands react by raising the discount.

I wouldn’t.

Here’s how I’d plan it:

→ Don’t run 20% off sitewide. Use “”up to”” framing, with the biggest discount on slow-moving stock and the smallest on your hero products
→ When revenue drops, add a second offer on top of the first instead of raising the discount. For example, the next 100 orders go into a draw, or the next 100 orders get a gift
→ Plan two or three of those offers before the sale starts, so you can launch one as soon as sales dip, because they will dip. #klaviyo

18111807644141857.caption:
Average monthly churn is one of the most common subscription metrics. It’s also not specific enough to be useful.

Here’s what I’d track instead:

- First order subscription take rate. How many people you get onto the subscription in the first place
- Order 2 retention
- Order 3 retention. If someone makes it to 3 orders, there’s a good chance they’ll stay for 6
- Contribution margin per customer

I wouldn’t lean on revenue per subscriber or average subscription duration.

Duration gets messy because people renew at different frequencies, weekly, fortnightly and so on. #klaviyo

18108225596205541.caption:
If you’re trying to increase lifetime value, attributed revenue in Klaviyo is the wrong number to look at.

Look at returning customer revenue from email and optimise for that.

A few other changes I’d make:

→ Instead of bigger sitewide discounts to get people buying more, use hand-picked bundles that lift AOV and work for your margins
→ Don’t give VIPs discounts. They’d already buy from you at full price. Give them perks instead, like early access to new products and restocks, and exclusive events
→ Don’t upsell customers before their product arrives. Give value first, then upsell once it’s in their hands. #klaviyo

18130800751868143.caption:
Most churn is decided in the first two weeks of a subscription.

That’s when people either build the habit of using the product properly, or they don’t.

If I’m working on churn for a subscription brand, here’s where I’d spend the time:

- An onboarding flow that helps people build that habit in the first two weeks
- A billing reminder flow. For a lot of brands this is the biggest cause of churn, so it has to be done well
- A splash page offer when someone goes to cancel. This recovers a lot of people
- Pamphlets in the packaging, so people have the information they need to use the product consistently
- Product quality

What I wouldn’t prioritise: win back flows, surprise and delight flows and payment failed flows.

Win back is you trying to get people back after you’ve already lost them. Most of the work should happen before that point. #klaviyo

17865305877695231.caption:
The job of your billing reminder email is to not cause a cancellation.

We’re happy if the customer takes no action from it at all.

Here’s how I’d set it up:

1. Don’t just put a cancel button in it. Give people the option to skip or delay their next order
2. Don’t make it all about the upcoming charge. Build excitement and remind them of the benefits they signed up for
3. Don’t add an SMS reminder on top. One email is enough
4. Don’t judge it on revenue. Track how many people cancel after receiving it and work to bring that number down. #klaviyo

17940226236392416.caption:
Ideally people never get as far as your cancellation page. But some will, and a few things make a big difference there.

What I’d set up:

1. A cancellation splash page. It’s good at recovering people who were about to cancel
2. Pause or delay options
3. A cancellation reason survey. You learn why people leave, pre-solve those reasons in onboarding, and personalise how you follow up with each person
4. Personalised cancellation offers

What I wouldn’t do:

→ Offer everyone the same discount to stay. People cancel for different reasons
→ Run an email win back sequence straight after. These people have already checked out
→ Make cancelling harder. It’s borderline illegal, and it kills any chance of reactivating that customer later. #klaviyo

18149172214564642.caption:
10% off isn’t much of a reason to sign up to a recurring subscription.

But jumping straight to a bigger discount isn’t the answer either.

Here’s what I’d do:

1. Stack different offers, like a free gift, free shipping and a small discount
2. Before going deeper on the discount, compare the contribution margin of subscribers at 3 to 6 months with your one-time customers. That tells you what you can actually afford
3. Don’t put every freebie on order one. Space the gifts out over a few months so people have to stay subscribed to get them
4. Don’t offer a price guarantee. Guarantee stock instead, so subscribers get first allocation. It also gives a bit of FOMO that your product might sell out. #klaviyo

18349460830284116.caption:
People on your subscription are already paying you every month.

You don’t need to keep selling to them.

Things that hurt:
→ Sending them 20 campaigns a month
→ Sending them every sale
→ Sending the same email to everyone on your list

Things that help:
→ A subscriber-only newsletter
→ Recipes and usage tips
→ Exclusive cross-sell offers
→ Excluding active subscribers from your prospect campaigns

Most of what they get from you should help them use the product, not push another sale. #klaviyo

18123909230473615.caption:
Giveaways grow your list, but not with people who want to buy.

I’d rather focus on converting the traffic that’s already on your site with the intention to purchase.

Two other pop-up changes:

- Don’t just offer 10% off and leave it there. Treat 10% as your baseline and test other offers to see if anything beats it
- Don’t show the discount upfront. Get people to take a small action first, a micro-commitment, to reveal the code. #klaviyo

17939150982399952.caption:
If you want more first orders going onto subscription, a deeper discount is usually the wrong lever.

It just hurts your contribution margin. A 10% subscription discount on its own doesn’t do much either.

What actually moves take rate:

→ The subscription offer itself
→ Cadence options, so people can pick a delivery frequency that suits them. This one is very important
→ Saying “”cancel anytime”” loudly
→ Pushing the subscription offer in your pop-up, campaigns and flows, not just on the product page

One thing I’d avoid is stacking all the freebies on order one.

People subscribe, get everything on the first order, then cancel straight away. #klaviyo

Your sales copy doesn’t need to sound more impressive. It needs to sound more human.

7 simple changes can make a big difference:

* Replace vague promises with specific outcomes.
* Show real benefits, not just features.
* Use proof instead of exaggerated claims.
* Answer questions before customers ask.
* Make your message relatable.
* Use clear, helpful CTAs.

18078260849732630.caption:
"You don't need every flow Klaviyo offers. Most of the revenue comes from a handful.

The ones I'd make sure are built properly:

1. Welcome flow. Every new subscriber goes into this
2. Abandoned cart
3. Browse abandonment
4. Site abandonment
5. Post purchase. If I had to pick one, it's this

Back in stock is worth it if you have hundreds or thousands of SKUs. Otherwise not really.

The ones I wouldn't spend time on yet: birthday, sunset, win back and VIP flows.

And you don't need a separate review flow. The review ask should already be in your post purchase flow." #klaviyo

18108387416203232.caption:
“You can sell the dream in your ads.

But once someone has bought, you need to be realistic about what they’ll get and when. Otherwise they cancel as soon as it doesn’t match what they were sold.

What I’d focus on in onboarding:

1. Setting realistic expectations
2. Teaching people how to use the product properly
3. Helping them build a daily habit with it
4. A welcome video from the founder. This one actually makes a difference

What I wouldn’t worry about: thank you emails, adding more emails after delivery, or fancy email designs.” #klaviyo

18131439418885458.caption:
“Most win back emails are a generic “”we miss you””. There’s no real reason in there to come back.

Here’s what I’d do instead:

1. Tell people what’s new, so there’s a genuine reason to be interested in your brand again
2. Don’t send every cancelled subscriber a discount. Ask why they cancelled and personalise your response to that reason
3. Skip the heavily designed email. Send a plain text note or a video from the founder

And don’t rely on a win back flow to increase lifetime value.

Pre-solve the reasons people churn, so fewer of them ever get to the point where you need to win them back.” #klaviyo

18150142528571034.caption:
“Black Friday works differently when a big part of your revenue is recurring subscriptions.

Give existing subscribers a sitewide discount and a lot of them will cancel their subscription and buy at the Black Friday price instead.

Here’s how I’d approach it:

→ Gifting offers. Buy more so you can give it to friends and family. This is the angle I’d take for most people on a subscription
→ Subscriber exclusive offers, with cross-sell items that actually add value
→ Add-on products in their next shipment

What I’d avoid:

→ Discounting their existing subscription orders
→ Excluding subscribers from every sale
→ Daily sale reminders to subscribers. This actively hurts you” #klaviyo

18395526325163908.caption:
“Don’t sell a one-time purchase and hope people love the product enough to come back and subscribe.

Push the subscription everywhere, in your funnels and your flows, and keep one-time purchase as the downsell for people who aren’t ready to commit.

A few other things that work:

- Don’t deepen the discount to get subscribers. Offer a stack of incentives that drips out over months, so people subscribe and have a reason to stay subscribed
- Don’t blast active subscribers with campaigns. Only send them information that helps them get better results from the product
- Don’t rely only on Meta and your product page. Build a dedicated post-purchase journey that turns one-time buyers into subscribers” #klaviyo

18140028781730270.caption:
“The quickest way to lift subscription take rate on a product page is to pre-select the subscription option.

That alone usually moves it straight away.

A few others that help:
- Show how much they save by subscribing
- Show the free gifts they get
- Match the delivery frequency to how fast people actually use the product

That last one matters most for churn.

If you deliver 60 days of product every 30 days, no email flow or strategy is going to fix your churn.

What doesn’t matter: button colours, fancy product descriptions, or making one-time purchase hard to find.” #klaviyo

17889134613488258.caption:
“If you’re judging your subscription program on Klaviyo attributed revenue, you’re tracking the wrong thing.

Use the churn data in Skio or Recharge to see how your strategies are actually affecting churn.

Three other changes:

- Don’t track average monthly churn. Look at retention for each individual order, fix the biggest bottleneck, then move on to the next one
- Don’t judge your billing reminder flow on revenue. Track how many cancellations it causes and work to bring that down
- Don’t track total subscribers. Track how many make it to their third or fourth order” #klaviyo

18096730391168783.caption:
“Billing reminders do increase churn. That’s just the reality of them.

The job is to test and reduce how much churn they cause.

What I’d put in a billing reminder:
- Clear information about the upcoming charge. This is legally required anyway
- A reminder of the benefits they’re getting
- Any free gifts coming up in their next order
- Personalisation by product

What I wouldn’t do:
- Leave the default reminder templates as they are
- Hide the cancel button. It’s bad practice and probably illegal

Then test how every change affects churn.” #klaviyo

18033259568886282.caption:
“A lot of subscription churn happens in the first few orders. Here’s 4 changes that help.

1. Don’t lead with a discount to get people onto the subscription
Announce a free gift the day box one lands, so they have a reason to stay for the next order.

2. Don’t wait for subscribers to pause or cancel
Offer them the chance to delay their next order so they can finish what they have before the next box arrives.

3. Don’t go quiet after the first order
Send a clear results timeline so they know what to expect after order one, two and three.

4. Don’t send the same “”update your card”” email every time a payment fails
Personalise it by how many times the card has declined. Once or twice could be an accident. Three or four times, treat them like a churned customer you’re trying to win back.” #klaviyo

18133626571752577.caption:

When you're stuck on what to offer for Black Friday, it's easy to fall back on 10% off sitewide because it feels safe. That's where the problem starts and it's why I call it the 10% problem.

Why 10% falls flat
➡️ It's the same discount most brands give on their signup form for a first purchase
➡️ Your customer has seen it all year, so it doesn't feel like Black Friday
➡️ It gets lost next to every competitor shouting bigger numbers

How to fix it without wrecking your margins
➡️ Break your margins down product by product, not just at the top level
➡️ Look for a collection you can discount further
➡️ Pick a few key products that can carry a bigger discount
➡️ Keep the smaller discount on everything else

Change the message
➡️ "10% off" becomes "up to 20% off"
➡️ Same business, a far more exciting offer

Most founders find room for this straight away. We get so focused on top-level margins that we miss the flexibility already sitting in the business.

The offer amount matters for your business. The messaging behind it is what drives your sales.

In the full video I walk through all 3 offers I build into every Black Friday strategy, plus how to work out your public offer first.

17906988654669310.caption:
People on your subscription are already paying you every month.

You don’t need to keep selling to them.

Things that hurt:
→ Sending them 20 campaigns a month
→ Sending them every sale
→ Sending the same email to everyone on your list

Things that help:
→ A subscriber-only newsletter
→ Recipes and usage tips
→ Exclusive cross-sell offers
→ Excluding active subscribers from your prospect campaigns

Most of what they get from you should help them use the product, not push another sale. #klaviyo

18107424491371296.caption:
“Giveaways grow your list, but not with people who want to buy.

I’d rather focus on converting the traffic that’s already on your site with the intention to purchase.

Two other pop-up changes:

- Don’t just offer 10% off and leave it there. Treat 10% as your baseline and test other offers to see if anything beats it
- Don’t show the discount upfront. Get people to take a small action first, a micro-commitment, to reveal the code” #klaviyo

18119812147785805.caption:
“Most churn is decided in the first two weeks of a subscription.

That’s when people either build the habit of using the product properly, or they don’t.

If I’m working on churn for a subscription brand, here’s where I’d spend the time:

- An onboarding flow that helps people build that habit in the first two weeks
- A billing reminder flow. For a lot of brands this is the biggest cause of churn, so it has to be done well
- A splash page offer when someone goes to cancel. This recovers a lot of people
- Pamphlets in the packaging, so people have the information they need to use the product consistently
- Product quality

What I wouldn’t prioritise: win back flows, surprise and delight flows and payment failed flows.

Win back is you trying to get people back after you’ve already lost them. Most of the work should happen before that point.” #klaviyo

18096378776449010.caption:
“The job of your billing reminder email is to not cause a cancellation.

We’re happy if the customer takes no action from it at all.

Here’s how I’d set it up:

1. Don’t just put a cancel button in it. Give people the option to skip or delay their next order
2. Don’t make it all about the upcoming charge. Build excitement and remind them of the benefits they signed up for
3. Don’t add an SMS reminder on top. One email is enough
4. Don’t judge it on revenue. Track how many people cancel after receiving it and work to bring that number down” #klaviyo

18112308719110428.caption:
“If you want more first orders going onto subscription, a deeper discount is usually the wrong lever.

It just hurts your contribution margin. A 10% subscription discount on its own doesn’t do much either.

What actually moves take rate:

→ The subscription offer itself
→ Cadence options, so people can pick a delivery frequency that suits them. This one is very important
→ Saying “”cancel anytime”” loudly
→ Pushing the subscription offer in your pop-up, campaigns and flows, not just on the product page

One thing I’d avoid is stacking all the freebies on order one.

People subscribe, get everything on the first order, then cancel straight away.” #klaviyo

18120252260077548.caption:
“Around day four of a Black Friday sale, revenue usually drops back to normal. A lot of brands react by raising the discount.

I wouldn’t.

Here’s how I’d plan it:

→ Don’t run 20% off sitewide. Use “”up to”” framing, with the biggest discount on slow-moving stock and the smallest on your hero products
→ When revenue drops, add a second offer on top of the first instead of raising the discount. For example, the next 100 orders go into a draw, or the next 100 orders get a gift
→ Plan two or three of those offers before the sale starts, so you can launch one as soon as sales dip, because they will dip” #klaviyo

18097808174664474.caption:
“Getting a brand to $3M a year doesn’t need an advanced email setup.

Most of what people obsess over at this stage doesn’t matter yet.

What does matter:
- Welcome flow
- Abandoned cart
- Consistent campaigns
- Optimising the pop-up
- Send time optimisation
- Advanced segmentation

What doesn’t:
- Birthday flows
- Hyper personalisation
- A/B testing subject lines
- Building 15 flows
- A loyalty program
- A sunset flow. You don’t need to email unengaged people, you can just suppress them

Same with deliverability. You’re not sending enough volume at this stage for it to be a real worry.

Just don’t do anything stupid and you’ll be fine.” #klaviyo

18132687691827680.caption:
“10% off isn’t much of a reason to sign up to a recurring subscription.

But jumping straight to a bigger discount isn’t the answer either.

Here’s what I’d do:

1. Stack different offers, like a free gift, free shipping and a small discount
2. Before going deeper on the discount, compare the contribution margin of subscribers at 3 to 6 months with your one-time customers. That tells you what you can actually afford
3. Don’t put every freebie on order one. Space the gifts out over a few months so people have to stay subscribed to get them
4. Don’t offer a price guarantee. Guarantee stock instead, so subscribers get first allocation. It also gives a bit of FOMO that your product might sell out” #klaviyo

17877392289583809.caption:
“Ideally people never get as far as your cancellation page. But some will, and a few things make a big difference there.

What I’d set up:

1. A cancellation splash page. It’s good at recovering people who were about to cancel
2. Pause or delay options
3. A cancellation reason survey. You learn why people leave, pre-solve those reasons in onboarding, and personalise how you follow up with each person
4. Personalised cancellation offers

What I wouldn’t do:

→ Offer everyone the same discount to stay. People cancel for different reasons
→ Run an email win back sequence straight after. These people have already checked out
→ Make cancelling harder. It’s borderline illegal, and it kills any chance of reactivating that customer later” #klaviyo

18115195295334362.caption:
“If you’re trying to increase lifetime value, attributed revenue in Klaviyo is the wrong number to look at.

Look at returning customer revenue from email and optimise for that.

A few other changes I’d make:

→ Instead of bigger sitewide discounts to get people buying more, use hand-picked bundles that lift AOV and work for your margins
→ Don’t give VIPs discounts. They’d already buy from you at full price. Give them perks instead, like early access to new products and restocks, and exclusive events
→ Don’t upsell customers before their product arrives. Give value first, then upsell once it’s in their hands” #klaviyo

18114366637895024.caption:
“Average monthly churn is one of the most common subscription metrics. It’s also not specific enough to be useful.

Here’s what I’d track instead:

- First order subscription take rate. How many people you get onto the subscription in the first place
- Order 2 retention
- Order 3 retention. If someone makes it to 3 orders, there’s a good chance they’ll stay for 6
- Contribution margin per customer

I wouldn’t lean on revenue per subscriber or average subscription duration.

Duration gets messy because people renew at different frequencies, weekly, fortnightly and so on.” #klaviyo

18452216245135342.caption:
Giveaways grow your list, but not with people who want to buy.

I’d rather focus on converting the traffic that’s already on your site with the intention to purchase.

Two other pop-up changes:

- Don’t just offer 10% off and leave it there. Treat 10% as your baseline and test other offers to see if anything beats it
- Don’t show the discount upfront. Get people to take a small action first, a micro-commitment, to reveal the code. #klaviyo

18176610922455579.caption:
The quickest way to lift subscription take rate on a product page is to pre-select the subscription option.

That alone usually moves it straight away.

A few others that help:
- Show how much they save by subscribing
- Show the free gifts they get
- Match the delivery frequency to how fast people actually use the product

That last one matters most for churn.

If you deliver 60 days of product every 30 days, no email flow or strategy is going to fix your churn.

What doesn’t matter: button colours, fancy product descriptions, or making one-time purchase hard to find. #klaviyo

18000068487032426.caption:
Most win back emails are a generic “”we miss you””. There’s no real reason in there to come back.

Here’s what I’d do instead:

1. Tell people what’s new, so there’s a genuine reason to be interested in your brand again
2. Don’t send every cancelled subscriber a discount. Ask why they cancelled and personalise your response to that reason
3. Skip the heavily designed email. Send a plain text note or a video from the founder

And don’t rely on a win back flow to increase lifetime value.

Pre-solve the reasons people churn, so fewer of them ever get to the point where you need to win them back. #klaviyo

18114997499465029.caption:
What gets you from $3M to $10M a year is lifetime value.

So the number I’d watch in Klaviyo is returning customer revenue. Not attributed revenue, and not new customer revenue.

The other things that matter at this stage:

→ First to second order conversion
→ VIP segment growth
→ Incrementality testing
→ Deliverability. You’re now sending enough volume that it’s a real risk, so you have to look after it
→ A proper segmentation strategy, which helps deliverability and returning customer revenue at the same time

Birthday flows still don’t matter here. #klaviyo

18570637450074122.caption:
A lot of subscription churn happens in the first few orders. Here’s 4 changes that help.

1. Don’t lead with a discount to get people onto the subscription
Announce a free gift the day box one lands, so they have a reason to stay for the next order.

2. Don’t wait for subscribers to pause or cancel
Offer them the chance to delay their next order so they can finish what they have before the next box arrives.

3. Don’t go quiet after the first order
Send a clear results timeline so they know what to expect after order one, two and three.

4. Don’t send the same “”update your card”” email every time a payment fails
Personalise it by how many times the card has declined. Once or twice could be an accident. Three or four times, treat them like a churned customer you’re trying to win back. #klaviyo

18115321928585788.caption:
You can sell the dream in your ads.

But once someone has bought, you need to be realistic about what they’ll get and when. Otherwise they cancel as soon as it doesn’t match what they were sold.

What I’d focus on in onboarding:

1. Setting realistic expectations
2. Teaching people how to use the product properly
3. Helping them build a daily habit with it
4. A welcome video from the founder. This one actually makes a difference

What I wouldn’t worry about: thank you emails, adding more emails after delivery, or fancy email designs. #klaviyo

18080679791393293.caption:
If you’re judging your subscription program on Klaviyo attributed revenue, you’re tracking the wrong thing.

Use the churn data in Skio or Recharge to see how your strategies are actually affecting churn.

Three other changes:

- Don’t track average monthly churn. Look at retention for each individual order, fix the biggest bottleneck, then move on to the next one
- Don’t judge your billing reminder flow on revenue. Track how many cancellations it causes and work to bring that down
- Don’t track total subscribers. Track how many make it to their third or fourth order. #klaviyo

18007572366006508.caption:
You don’t need every flow Klaviyo offers. Most of the revenue comes from a handful.

The ones I’d make sure are built properly:

1. Welcome flow. Every new subscriber goes into this
2. Abandoned cart
3. Browse abandonment
4. Site abandonment
5. Post purchase. If I had to pick one, it’s this

Back in stock is worth it if you have hundreds or thousands of SKUs. Otherwise not really.

The ones I wouldn’t spend time on yet: birthday, sunset, win back and VIP flows.

And you don’t need a separate review flow. The review ask should already be in your post purchase flow.  #klaviyo

17954052063301632.caption:
Don’t sell a one-time purchase and hope people love the product enough to come back and subscribe.

Push the subscription everywhere, in your funnels and your flows, and keep one-time purchase as the downsell for people who aren’t ready to commit.

A few other things that work:

- Don’t deepen the discount to get subscribers. Offer a stack of incentives that drips out over months, so people subscribe and have a reason to stay subscribed
- Don’t blast active subscribers with campaigns. Only send them information that helps them get better results from the product
- Don’t rely only on Meta and your product page. Build a dedicated post-purchase journey that turns one-time buyers into subscribers.  #klaviyo

18093229499300808.caption:
Black Friday works differently when a big part of your revenue is recurring subscriptions.

Give existing subscribers a sitewide discount and a lot of them will cancel their subscription and buy at the Black Friday price instead.

Here’s how I’d approach it:

→ Gifting offers. Buy more so you can give it to friends and family. This is the angle I’d take for most people on a subscription
→ Subscriber exclusive offers, with cross-sell items that actually add value
→ Add-on products in their next shipment

What I’d avoid:

→ Discounting their existing subscription orders
→ Excluding subscribers from every sale
→ Daily sale reminders to subscribers. This actively hurts you. #klaviyo

18116084270026075.caption:
Comment “GREEN” to get 30% off omnisend for your first 3 months.

Your Black Friday sale has an end date. Your emails should make people feel it.

Urgency is what turns “I’ll come back later” into a click.

A countdown timer shows subscribers exactly how long they have left and adding one to your campaigns can lift your click-through rate by up to 25%.

In the busiest week of the year in the inbox, that’s the difference between someone buying now and someone forgetting about your sale altogether.

A timer also brings movement into your email and movement in emails really does work. It’s the same reason GIFs work so well.

That’s why I recommend putting your timer in the hero section. The moment someone opens your email they see something moving, which grabs their attention and draws them down into the rest of the email.

Save it for the emails where time is actually running out: the end of early access, the final days of your sale and the last hours before it closes.

#omnisend #emailmarketing

18002332110013024.caption:
Don’t sell a one-time purchase and hope people love the product enough to come back and subscribe.

Push the subscription everywhere, in your funnels and your flows, and keep one-time purchase as the downsell for people who aren’t ready to commit.

A few other things that work:

- Don’t deepen the discount to get subscribers. Offer a stack of incentives that drips out over months, so people subscribe and have a reason to stay subscribed
- Don’t blast active subscribers with campaigns. Only send them information that helps them get better results from the product
- Don’t rely only on Meta and your product page. Build a dedicated post-purchase journey that turns one-time buyers into subscribers. #klaviyo

18098297150151114.caption:
Most churn is decided in the first two weeks of a subscription.

That’s when people either build the habit of using the product properly, or they don’t.

If I’m working on churn for a subscription brand, here’s where I’d spend the time:

- An onboarding flow that helps people build that habit in the first two weeks
- A billing reminder flow. For a lot of brands this is the biggest cause of churn, so it has to be done well
- A splash page offer when someone goes to cancel. This recovers a lot of people
- Pamphlets in the packaging, so people have the information they need to use the product consistently
- Product quality

What I wouldn’t prioritise: win back flows, surprise and delight flows and payment failed flows.

Win back is you trying to get people back after you’ve already lost them. Most of the work should happen before that point. #klaviyo

18364244152222842.caption:
10% off isn’t much of a reason to sign up to a recurring subscription.

But jumping straight to a bigger discount isn’t the answer either.

Here’s what I’d do:

1. Stack different offers, like a free gift, free shipping and a small discount
2. Before going deeper on the discount, compare the contribution margin of subscribers at 3 to 6 months with your one-time customers. That tells you what you can actually afford
3. Don’t put every freebie on order one. Space the gifts out over a few months so people have to stay subscribed to get them
4. Don’t offer a price guarantee. Guarantee stock instead, so subscribers get first allocation. It also gives a bit of FOMO that your product might sell out. #klaviyo

18399689905160709.caption:
Average monthly churn is one of the most common subscription metrics. It’s also not specific enough to be useful.

Here’s what I’d track instead:

- First order subscription take rate. How many people you get onto the subscription in the first place
- Order 2 retention
- Order 3 retention. If someone makes it to 3 orders, there’s a good chance they’ll stay for 6
- Contribution margin per customer

I wouldn’t lean on revenue per subscriber or average subscription duration.

Duration gets messy because people renew at different frequencies, weekly, fortnightly and so on. #klaviyo

18102151532646495.caption:
Around day four of a Black Friday sale, revenue usually drops back to normal. A lot of brands react by raising the discount.

I wouldn’t.

Here’s how I’d plan it:

→ Don’t run 20% off sitewide. Use “”up to”” framing, with the biggest discount on slow-moving stock and the smallest on your hero products
→ When revenue drops, add a second offer on top of the first instead of raising the discount. For example, the next 100 orders go into a draw, or the next 100 orders get a gift
→ Plan two or three of those offers before the sale starts, so you can launch one as soon as sales dip, because they will dip.  #klaviyo

18212322037366794.caption:
Getting a brand to $3M a year doesn’t need an advanced email setup.

Most of what people obsess over at this stage doesn’t matter yet.

What does matter:
- Welcome flow
- Abandoned cart
- Consistent campaigns
- Optimising the pop-up
- Send time optimisation
- Advanced segmentation

What doesn’t:
- Birthday flows
- Hyper personalisation
- A/B testing subject lines
- Building 15 flows
- A loyalty program
- A sunset flow. You don’t need to email unengaged people, you can just suppress them

Same with deliverability. You’re not sending enough volume at this stage for it to be a real worry.

Just don’t do anything stupid and you’ll be fine. #klaviyo

18127623559911747.caption:
The job of your billing reminder email is to not cause a cancellation.

We’re happy if the customer takes no action from it at all.

Here’s how I’d set it up:

1. Don’t just put a cancel button in it. Give people the option to skip or delay their next order
2. Don’t make it all about the upcoming charge. Build excitement and remind them of the benefits they signed up for
3. Don’t add an SMS reminder on top. One email is enough
4. Don’t judge it on revenue. Track how many people cancel after receiving it and work to bring that number down. #klaviyo

18111398360175776.caption:
Ideally people never get as far as your cancellation page. But some will, and a few things make a big difference there.

What I’d set up:

1. A cancellation splash page. It’s good at recovering people who were about to cancel
2. Pause or delay options
3. A cancellation reason survey. You learn why people leave, pre-solve those reasons in onboarding, and personalise how you follow up with each person
4. Personalised cancellation offers

What I wouldn’t do:

→ Offer everyone the same discount to stay. People cancel for different reasons
→ Run an email win back sequence straight after. These people have already checked out
→ Make cancelling harder. It’s borderline illegal, and it kills any chance of reactivating that customer later. #klaviyo

18126312935293973.caption:
If you’re trying to increase lifetime value, attributed revenue in Klaviyo is the wrong number to look at.

Look at returning customer revenue from email and optimise for that.

A few other changes I’d make:

→ Instead of bigger sitewide discounts to get people buying more, use hand-picked bundles that lift AOV and work for your margins
→ Don’t give VIPs discounts. They’d already buy from you at full price. Give them perks instead, like early access to new products and restocks, and exclusive events
→ Don’t upsell customers before their product arrives. Give value first, then upsell once it’s in their hands. #klaviyo

18452878018120063.caption:
If you want more first orders going onto subscription, a deeper discount is usually the wrong lever.

It just hurts your contribution margin. A 10% subscription discount on its own doesn’t do much either.

What actually moves take rate:

→ The subscription offer itself
→ Cadence options, so people can pick a delivery frequency that suits them. This one is very important
→ Saying “”cancel anytime”” loudly
→ Pushing the subscription offer in your pop-up, campaigns and flows, not just on the product page

One thing I’d avoid is stacking all the freebies on order one.

People subscribe, get everything on the first order, then cancel straight away. #klaviyo

17987412537109341.caption:
Giveaways grow your list, but not with people who want to buy.

I’d rather focus on converting the traffic that’s already on your site with the intention to purchase.

Two other pop-up changes:

- Don’t just offer 10% off and leave it there. Treat 10% as your baseline and test other offers to see if anything beats it
- Don’t show the discount upfront. Get people to take a small action first, a micro-commitment, to reveal the code. #klaviyo

18115640441616593.caption:
Black Friday works differently when a big part of your revenue is recurring subscriptions.

Give existing subscribers a sitewide discount and a lot of them will cancel their subscription and buy at the Black Friday price instead.

Here’s how I’d approach it:

→ Gifting offers. Buy more so you can give it to friends and family. This is the angle I’d take for most people on a subscription
→ Subscriber exclusive offers, with cross-sell items that actually add value
→ Add-on products in their next shipment

What I’d avoid:

→ Discounting their existing subscription orders
→ Excluding subscribers from every sale
→ Daily sale reminders to subscribers. This actively hurts you. #klaviyo

18118246517278969.caption:
If you’re trying to increase lifetime value, attributed revenue in Klaviyo is the wrong number to look at.

Look at returning customer revenue from email and optimise for that.

A few other changes I’d make:

→ Instead of bigger sitewide discounts to get people buying more, use hand-picked bundles that lift AOV and work for your margins
→ Don’t give VIPs discounts. They’d already buy from you at full price. Give them perks instead, like early access to new products and restocks, and exclusive events
→ Don’t upsell customers before their product arrives. Give value first, then upsell once it’s in their hands. #klaviyo

18641848783031883.caption:
You can sell the dream in your ads.

But once someone has bought, you need to be realistic about what they'll get and when. Otherwise they cancel as soon as it doesn't match what they were sold.

What I'd focus on in onboarding:

1. Setting realistic expectations
2. Teaching people how to use the product properly
3. Helping them build a daily habit with it
4. A welcome video from the founder. This one actually makes a difference

What I wouldn't worry about: thank you emails, adding more emails after delivery, or fancy email designs. #klaviyo

18116044877277588.caption:
If you’re judging your subscription program on Klaviyo attributed revenue, you’re tracking the wrong thing.

Use the churn data in Skio or Recharge to see how your strategies are actually affecting churn.

Three other changes:

- Don’t track average monthly churn. Look at retention for each individual order, fix the biggest bottleneck, then move on to the next one
- Don’t judge your billing reminder flow on revenue. Track how many cancellations it causes and work to bring that down
- Don’t track total subscribers. Track how many make it to their third or fourth order. #klaviyo

17974293849160135.caption:
You don’t need every flow Klaviyo offers. Most of the revenue comes from a handful.

The ones I’d make sure are built properly:

1. Welcome flow. Every new subscriber goes into this
2. Abandoned cart
3. Browse abandonment
4. Site abandonment
5. Post purchase. If I had to pick one, it’s this

Back in stock is worth it if you have hundreds or thousands of SKUs. Otherwise not really.

The ones I wouldn’t spend time on yet: birthday, sunset, win back and VIP flows.

And you don’t need a separate review flow. The review ask should already be in your post purchase flow. #klaviyo

18209889466374219.caption:
A lot of subscription churn happens in the first few orders. Here’s 4 changes that help.

1. Don’t lead with a discount to get people onto the subscription
Announce a free gift the day box one lands, so they have a reason to stay for the next order.

2. Don’t wait for subscribers to pause or cancel
Offer them the chance to delay their next order so they can finish what they have before the next box arrives.

3. Don’t go quiet after the first order
Send a clear results timeline so they know what to expect after order one, two and three.

4. Don’t send the same “”update your card”” email every time a payment fails
Personalise it by how many times the card has declined. Once or twice could be an accident. Three or four times, treat them like a churned customer you’re trying to win back.

18002008362042243.caption:
What gets you from $3M to $10M a year is lifetime value.

So the number I’d watch in Klaviyo is returning customer revenue. Not attributed revenue, and not new customer revenue.

The other things that matter at this stage:

→ First to second order conversion
→ VIP segment growth
→ Incrementality testing
→ Deliverability. You’re now sending enough volume that it’s a real risk, so you have to look after it
→ A proper segmentation strategy, which helps deliverability and returning customer revenue at the same time

Birthday flows still don’t matter here. #klaviyo

18135864625813210.caption:
Most win back emails are a generic “”we miss you””. There’s no real reason in there to come back.

Here’s what I’d do instead:

1. Tell people what’s new, so there’s a genuine reason to be interested in your brand again
2. Don’t send every cancelled subscriber a discount. Ask why they cancelled and personalise your response to that reason
3. Skip the heavily designed email. Send a plain text note or a video from the founder

And don’t rely on a win back flow to increase lifetime value.

Pre-solve the reasons people churn, so fewer of them ever get to the point where you need to win them back. #klaviyo

18105684359339304.caption:
The quickest way to lift subscription take rate on a product page is to pre-select the subscription option.

That alone usually moves it straight away.

A few others that help:
- Show how much they save by subscribing
- Show the free gifts they get
- Match the delivery frequency to how fast people actually use the product

That last one matters most for churn.

If you deliver 60 days of product every 30 days, no email flow or strategy is going to fix your churn.

What doesn’t matter: button colours, fancy product descriptions, or making one-time purchase hard to find. #klaviyo

18120925990778251.caption:
6 mistakes that send your Black Friday emails to spam:

1. Mailing people who went cold in spring → win back or remove anyone inactive 90+ days

2. Spiking volume overnight → ramp up in steps, most engaged first

3. Sending from a brand-new domain → keep your domain and pass SPF, DKIM, DMARC

4. Hiding the unsubscribe → add one-click unsubscribe (Gmail wants it honored within 48 hours)

5. Using link shorteners → use links on your own domain

6. Checking complaints too late → check spam rate daily and stay under 0.1%

Go over 0.3% and Google won't help with delivery issues until you've stayed under it for 7 straight days.

Black Friday is Nov 27. Start these this week.

18180481111432064.caption:
“Don’t sell a one-time purchase and hope people love the product enough to come back and subscribe.

Push the subscription everywhere, in your funnels and your flows, and keep one-time purchase as the downsell for people who aren’t ready to commit.

A few other things that work:

- Don’t deepen the discount to get subscribers. Offer a stack of incentives that drips out over months, so people subscribe and have a reason to stay subscribed
- Don’t blast active subscribers with campaigns. Only send them information that helps them get better results from the product
- Don’t rely only on Meta and your product page. Build a dedicated post-purchase journey that turns one-time buyers into subscribers” #klaviyo

18358785829171582.caption:
“You can sell the dream in your ads.

But once someone has bought, you need to be realistic about what they’ll get and when. Otherwise they cancel as soon as it doesn’t match what they were sold.

What I’d focus on in onboarding:

1. Setting realistic expectations
2. Teaching people how to use the product properly
3. Helping them build a daily habit with it
4. A welcome video from the founder. This one actually makes a difference

What I wouldn’t worry about: thank you emails, adding more emails after delivery, or fancy email designs.” #klaviyo

18135333349815404.caption:
“What gets you from $3M to $10M a year is lifetime value.

So the number I’d watch in Klaviyo is returning customer revenue. Not attributed revenue, and not new customer revenue.

The other things that matter at this stage:

→ First to second order conversion
→ VIP segment growth
→ Incrementality testing
→ Deliverability. You’re now sending enough volume that it’s a real risk, so you have to look after it
→ A proper segmentation strategy, which helps deliverability and returning customer revenue at the same time

Birthday flows still don’t matter here.” #klaviyo

18339596728277787.caption:
“The quickest way to lift subscription take rate on a product page is to pre-select the subscription option.

That alone usually moves it straight away.

A few others that help:
- Show how much they save by subscribing
- Show the free gifts they get
- Match the delivery frequency to how fast people actually use the product

That last one matters most for churn.

If you deliver 60 days of product every 30 days, no email flow or strategy is going to fix your churn.

What doesn’t matter: button colours, fancy product descriptions, or making one-time purchase hard to find.” #klaviyo

18147346696564712.caption:
“People on your subscription are already paying you every month.

You don’t need to keep selling to them.

Things that hurt:
→ Sending them 20 campaigns a month
→ Sending them every sale
→ Sending the same email to everyone on your list

Things that help:
→ A subscriber-only newsletter
→ Recipes and usage tips
→ Exclusive cross-sell offers
→ Excluding active subscribers from your prospect campaigns

Most of what they get from you should help them use the product, not push another sale.” #klaviyo

18080645906736301.caption:
“If you want more first orders going onto subscription, a deeper discount is usually the wrong lever.

It just hurts your contribution margin. A 10% subscription discount on its own doesn’t do much either.

What actually moves take rate:

→ The subscription offer itself
→ Cadence options, so people can pick a delivery frequency that suits them. This one is very important
→ Saying “”cancel anytime”” loudly
→ Pushing the subscription offer in your pop-up, campaigns and flows, not just on the product page

One thing I’d avoid is stacking all the freebies on order one.

People subscribe, get everything on the first order, then cancel straight away.” #klaviyo

18116855132040197.caption:
“Billing reminders do increase churn. That’s just the reality of them.

The job is to test and reduce how much churn they cause.

What I’d put in a billing reminder:
- Clear information about the upcoming charge. This is legally required anyway
- A reminder of the benefits they’re getting
- Any free gifts coming up in their next order
- Personalisation by product

What I wouldn’t do:
- Leave the default reminder templates as they are
- Hide the cancel button. It’s bad practice and probably illegal

Then test how every change affects churn.” #klaviyo

17878705482634694.caption:
“Most churn is decided in the first two weeks of a subscription.

That’s when people either build the habit of using the product properly, or they don’t.

If I’m working on churn for a subscription brand, here’s where I’d spend the time:

- An onboarding flow that helps people build that habit in the first two weeks
- A billing reminder flow. For a lot of brands this is the biggest cause of churn, so it has to be done well
- A splash page offer when someone goes to cancel. This recovers a lot of people
- Pamphlets in the packaging, so people have the information they need to use the product consistently
- Product quality

What I wouldn’t prioritise: win back flows, surprise and delight flows and payment failed flows.

Win back is you trying to get people back after you’ve already lost them. Most of the work should happen before that point.” #klaviyo

18130998877882692.caption:
“Black Friday works differently when a big part of your revenue is recurring subscriptions.

Give existing subscribers a sitewide discount and a lot of them will cancel their subscription and buy at the Black Friday price instead.

Here’s how I’d approach it:

→ Gifting offers. Buy more so you can give it to friends and family. This is the angle I’d take for most people on a subscription
→ Subscriber exclusive offers, with cross-sell items that actually add value
→ Add-on products in their next shipment

What I’d avoid:

→ Discounting their existing subscription orders
→ Excluding subscribers from every sale
→ Daily sale reminders to subscribers. This actively hurts you” #klaviyo

18133145779871981.caption:
Average monthly churn is one of the most common subscription metrics. It’s also not specific enough to be useful.

Here’s what I’d track instead:

- First order subscription take rate. How many people you get onto the subscription in the first place
- Order 2 retention
- Order 3 retention. If someone makes it to 3 orders, there’s a good chance they’ll stay for 6
- Contribution margin per customer

I wouldn’t lean on revenue per subscriber or average subscription duration.

Duration gets messy because people renew at different frequencies, weekly, fortnightly and so on. #klaviyo

18171050776477696.caption:
Most win back emails are a generic “”we miss you””. There’s no real reason in there to come back.

Here’s what I’d do instead:

1. Tell people what’s new, so there’s a genuine reason to be interested in your brand again
2. Don’t send every cancelled subscriber a discount. Ask why they cancelled and personalise your response to that reason
3. Skip the heavily designed email. Send a plain text note or a video from the founder

And don’t rely on a win back flow to increase lifetime value.

Pre-solve the reasons people churn, so fewer of them ever get to the point where you need to win them back. #klaviyo

18100709306198842.caption:
Getting a brand to $3M a year doesn’t need an advanced email setup.

Most of what people obsess over at this stage doesn’t matter yet.

What does matter:
- Welcome flow
- Abandoned cart
- Consistent campaigns
- Optimising the pop-up
- Send time optimisation
- Advanced segmentation

What doesn’t:
- Birthday flows
- Hyper personalisation
- A/B testing subject lines
- Building 15 flows
- A loyalty program
- A sunset flow. You don’t need to email unengaged people, you can just suppress them

Same with deliverability. You’re not sending enough volume at this stage for it to be a real worry.

Just don’t do anything stupid and you’ll be fine. #klaviyo

18122310428058739.caption:
Around day four of a Black Friday sale, revenue usually drops back to normal. A lot of brands react by raising the discount.

I wouldn’t.

Here’s how I’d plan it:

→ Don’t run 20% off sitewide. Use “”up to”” framing, with the biggest discount on slow-moving stock and the smallest on your hero products
→ When revenue drops, add a second offer on top of the first instead of raising the discount. For example, the next 100 orders go into a draw, or the next 100 orders get a gift
→ Plan two or three of those offers before the sale starts, so you can launch one as soon as sales dip, because they will dip. #klaviyo

18098385011554642.caption:
Ideally people never get as far as your cancellation page. But some will, and a few things make a big difference there.

What I’d set up:

1. A cancellation splash page. It’s good at recovering people who were about to cancel
2. Pause or delay options
3. A cancellation reason survey. You learn why people leave, pre-solve those reasons in onboarding, and personalise how you follow up with each person
4. Personalised cancellation offers

What I wouldn’t do:

→ Offer everyone the same discount to stay. People cancel for different reasons
→ Run an email win back sequence straight after. These people have already checked out
→ Make cancelling harder. It’s borderline illegal, and it kills any chance of reactivating that customer later. #klaviyo

18111392381245285.caption:
The job of your billing reminder email is to not cause a cancellation.

We’re happy if the customer takes no action from it at all.

Here’s how I’d set it up:

1. Don’t just put a cancel button in it. Give people the option to skip or delay their next order
2. Don’t make it all about the upcoming charge. Build excitement and remind them of the benefits they signed up for
3. Don’t add an SMS reminder on top. One email is enough
4. Don’t judge it on revenue. Track how many people cancel after receiving it and work to bring that number down. #klaviyo

18038512682661674.caption:
10% off isn’t much of a reason to sign up to a recurring subscription.

But jumping straight to a bigger discount isn’t the answer either.

Here’s what I’d do:

1. Stack different offers, like a free gift, free shipping and a small discount
2. Before going deeper on the discount, compare the contribution margin of subscribers at 3 to 6 months with your one-time customers. That tells you what you can actually afford
3. Don’t put every freebie on order one. Space the gifts out over a few months so people have to stay subscribed to get them
4. Don’t offer a price guarantee. Guarantee stock instead, so subscribers get first allocation. It also gives a bit of FOMO that your product might sell out. #klaviyo

Comment “GREEN” to get 30% off omnisend for your first 3 months and get set up before Black Friday.

A standard discount pop up sits around a 5% submit rate. Gamified forms easily hit 10 to 15%, and Omnisend has just built 2 new gamification elements straight into the form builder, no third-party app needed.

Here’s why they work so well:

🎟️ Scratch card
It turns “give us your email for 10% off” into a moment. Scratching builds curiosity and once someone has put in the effort to reveal a prize, they want to claim it. You design the card yourself too, so it feels on brand instead of like every other pop-up.

🎁 Mystery box
3 boxes, 1 choice. Picking a box makes people feel in control and not knowing what’s inside is what gets the click. That click is a small yes before the bigger yes of handing over their email.

Both work for the same reason. Your visitors start playing before you ask them for anything, so by the time the email field shows up, they’re already invested and want to see what they’ve won.

With Black Friday traffic about to spike, that’s a lot of leads you don’t want to lose to a boring pop up.

The rule of 100 is simple. You advertise your stuff by doing 100 primary actions every day, for one hundred days in a row. That’s it.

Here’s what it looks like applied to each of the core four:

Warm Reach Outs: 100 reach outs per day
Example primary actions: email, text, direct message, calls, etc.

Post Content: 100 minutes per day making content.
Release at least one per day on a platform. As you get better, post even more.

Example primary actions: short and long videos or articles, podcasts, infographics, etc.

Cold Reach Outs: 100 reach outs per day
Example primary actions: email, text, direct message, cold call, flyers, etc.

As with all cold advertising, expect lower response rates, so use automation.

Paid Ads: 100 minutes per day making paid ads
Example primary actions: direct response media ads, direct mail, seminar, podcast spots, etc.

100 days straight of running those paid ads.

Why do combo meals sell so well?

Because people love feeling like they’re getting a better deal.

A burger costs $6.
Fries cost $3.
A drink costs $2.

Total: $11.

But bundle them together for $9, and suddenly customers feel they’re saving money while getting more.

This is called bundle pricing.

Instead of selling products one by one, package them together to increase the perceived value and encourage bigger purchases.

The lesson? Make customers feel they’re getting more for their money.

18148874794585869.caption:
Why does $9.99 feel cheaper than $10.00?

It’s called the left-digit effect.

People often focus on the first number they see. 

So $9.99 feels closer to $9 than $10, even though the difference is just one penny.

Same product. 
Almost the same price. 
Different perception.

That’s the power of pricing psychology. Sometimes, how you present a price matters just as much as the price itself.

18113558267630595.caption:
“I ranked 7 common ways brands try to reduce subscription churn.

The two I’d avoid are requiring a minimum of two orders, which drives up your CAC massively unless you have a phenomenal brand, and turning off the billing reminder flow. Turning off the reminder is borderline illegal and unethical.

Making it hard to cancel is close behind. It annoys people and ruins any chance of getting them back later.

Offering a gift on the second order is an easy win if a lot of people churn after their first order.

Sending zero campaigns to subscribers is actually not a terrible strategy, because campaigns do cause churn. I still wouldn’t go all the way to zero.

The two that matter most are having a really good product and a really good onboarding flow. A good onboarding flow deals with the reasons people cancel before they come up, and it noticeably increases the lifetime value of your subscribers.” #klaviyo

18182326777445343.caption:
“What gets you from $3M to $10M a year is lifetime value.

So the number I’d watch in Klaviyo is returning customer revenue. Not attributed revenue, and not new customer revenue.

The other things that matter at this stage:

→ First to second order conversion
→ VIP segment growth
→ Incrementality testing
→ Deliverability. You’re now sending enough volume that it’s a real risk, so you have to look after it
→ A proper segmentation strategy, which helps deliverability and returning customer revenue at the same time

Birthday flows still don’t matter here.” #klaviyo

18043214225832083.caption:
“Billing reminders do increase churn. That’s just the reality of them.

The job is to test and reduce how much churn they cause.

What I’d put in a billing reminder:
- Clear information about the upcoming charge. This is legally required anyway
- A reminder of the benefits they’re getting
- Any free gifts coming up in their next order
- Personalisation by product

What I wouldn’t do:
- Leave the default reminder templates as they are
- Hide the cancel button. It’s bad practice and probably illegal

Then test how every change affects churn.” #klaviyo

18121079840106964.caption:
“If you want more first orders going onto subscription, a deeper discount is usually the wrong lever.

It just hurts your contribution margin. A 10% subscription discount on its own doesn’t do much either.

What actually moves take rate:

→ The subscription offer itself
→ Cadence options, so people can pick a delivery frequency that suits them. This one is very important
→ Saying “”cancel anytime”” loudly
→ Pushing the subscription offer in your pop-up, campaigns and flows, not just on the product page

One thing I’d avoid is stacking all the freebies on order one.

People subscribe, get everything on the first order, then cancel straight away.” #klaviyo

18098716523658010.caption:
“A lot of subscription churn happens in the first few orders. Here’s 4 changes that help.

1. Don’t lead with a discount to get people onto the subscription
Announce a free gift the day box one lands, so they have a reason to stay for the next order.

2. Don’t wait for subscribers to pause or cancel
Offer them the chance to delay their next order so they can finish what they have before the next box arrives.

3. Don’t go quiet after the first order
Send a clear results timeline so they know what to expect after order one, two and three.

4. Don’t send the same “”update your card”” email every time a payment fails
Personalise it by how many times the card has declined. Once or twice could be an accident. Three or four times, treat them like a churned customer you’re trying to win back.” #klaviyo

18144015400623416.caption:
“Most churn is decided in the first two weeks of a subscription.

That’s when people either build the habit of using the product properly, or they don’t.

If I’m working on churn for a subscription brand, here’s where I’d spend the time:

- An onboarding flow that helps people build that habit in the first two weeks
- A billing reminder flow. For a lot of brands this is the biggest cause of churn, so it has to be done well
- A splash page offer when someone goes to cancel. This recovers a lot of people
- Pamphlets in the packaging, so people have the information they need to use the product consistently
- Product quality

What I wouldn’t prioritise: win back flows, surprise and delight flows and payment failed flows.

Win back is you trying to get people back after you’ve already lost them. Most of the work should happen before that point.” #klaviyo

18133751563801633.caption:
“If you’re judging your subscription program on Klaviyo attributed revenue, you’re tracking the wrong thing.

Use the churn data in Skio or Recharge to see how your strategies are actually affecting churn.

Three other changes:

- Don’t track average monthly churn. Look at retention for each individual order, fix the biggest bottleneck, then move on to the next one
- Don’t judge your billing reminder flow on revenue. Track how many cancellations it causes and work to bring that down
- Don’t track total subscribers. Track how many make it to their third or fourth order” #klaviyo

18111363976920290.caption:
“The quickest way to lift subscription take rate on a product page is to pre-select the subscription option.

That alone usually moves it straight away.

A few others that help:
- Show how much they save by subscribing
- Show the free gifts they get
- Match the delivery frequency to how fast people actually use the product

That last one matters most for churn.

If you deliver 60 days of product every 30 days, no email flow or strategy is going to fix your churn.

What doesn’t matter: button colours, fancy product descriptions, or making one-time purchase hard to find.” #klaviyo

18081770723452241.caption:
“You don’t need every flow Klaviyo offers. Most of the revenue comes from a handful.

The ones I’d make sure are built properly:

1. Welcome flow. Every new subscriber goes into this
2. Abandoned cart
3. Browse abandonment
4. Site abandonment
5. Post purchase. If I had to pick one, it’s this

Back in stock is worth it if you have hundreds or thousands of SKUs. Otherwise not really.

The ones I wouldn’t spend time on yet: birthday, sunset, win back and VIP flows.

And you don’t need a separate review flow. The review ask should already be in your post purchase flow.” #klaviyo

18098591906668518.caption:
“People on your subscription are already paying you every month.

You don’t need to keep selling to them.

Things that hurt:
→ Sending them 20 campaigns a month
→ Sending them every sale
→ Sending the same email to everyone on your list

Things that help:
→ A subscriber-only newsletter
→ Recipes and usage tips
→ Exclusive cross-sell offers
→ Excluding active subscribers from your prospect campaigns

Most of what they get from you should help them use the product, not push another sale.” #klaviyo

17940883461122500.caption:
“You can sell the dream in your ads.

But once someone has bought, you need to be realistic about what they’ll get and when. Otherwise they cancel as soon as it doesn’t match what they were sold.

What I’d focus on in onboarding:

1. Setting realistic expectations
2. Teaching people how to use the product properly
3. Helping them build a daily habit with it
4. A welcome video from the founder. This one actually makes a difference

What I wouldn’t worry about: thank you emails, adding more emails after delivery, or fancy email designs.” #klaviyo
